subject: Public Affairs
description: An overview of management in not-for-profit organizations, with an emphasis on the role of leadership and styles of leadership.  Topics include techniques for board development, strategic planning, marketing and other aspects of not-for-profit management. Offered: fall only.

subject: Public Affairs
description: Addresses the changing role/environment of not-for-profit organizations.  Issues may include competition for financial and human resources, advancements in technology, increased mobility in a global environment, and the changing nature of public-private partnerships.  Offered: spring only.

subject: Public Affairs
description: This course introduces students to the structure and operation of nongovernmental organizations outside the United States. Students will learn how the differences in legal foundations, funding sources, and organization capacities affect mission and performance. Offered: periodically.

subject: Public Affairs
description: It is highly important that nonprofit professionals learn about revenue development and marketing. Without steady sources of income and brand awareness, a nonprofit will not be able to effectively enact its mission and programming. This course will provide a broad overview of nonprofit fundraising and marketing including an introduction to the theories and practices of charitable fundraising such as fundraising traditions in the U.S., philosophies of giving and asking, theories of donor motivation, and the organizational, legal, and ethical contexts of charitable fundraising. It reviews practical elements of fundraising plan development, as well as traditional and digital marketing methods to spread brand awareness and encourage engagement with and donations to their organization. Students are introduced to and gain practice using basic fundraising tools, including annual funds, special events, major gifts, planned giving, and capital campaigns.  Students will develop a fundraising and marketing plan including a fundraising goal, activities, and staffing.  Offered: Summer.

subject: Public Affairs
description: An in depth examination of issues or problems concerned with the theory and practice of not-for-profit management.  Topics vary; may be repeated for credit. Offered:   periodically.

subject: Public Affairs
description: The study of supranational governing systems and their effects, and how domestic public administration/policy responds to a new political order and global economy. Topics include NGOs, security arrangements, trade, environmental and labor agreements, international treaties, organizations and governing bodies such as WTO, Kyoto, UN, NAFTA, EU.

subject: Public Affairs
description: The course will examine the lives and experiences of migrant individuals and communities, especially in relation to discourses of belonging and citizenship, from a social justice perspective. A specific feature is the emphasis on the interconnectedness of global, regional, national, and local realities, as they affect the lives of people in everyday domains. While policies at the local, national, and transnational levels as well as issues around their effective, and just, implementation, are necessarily salient topics for the course, we are especially concerned with conceptualizing immigrants as social actors, who attempt to actualize their desires and intentions within constraints created by multi-layered power structures. From such a perspective, immigrants faced with injustices are not cast as passive victims, but as active agents of change, negotiating, and at times, challenging obstacles to dignified survival. Through readings, films, discussions, lectures (including guest lectures), and field research experiences, the course seeks to explore a range of issues in relation to social in/justice and migration, such as, the construction of the migrant as the ?Other?; the racial and gender dimensions of anti-immigrant discourse; discriminatory national, regional, and local policies and laws; barriers to quality healthcare and other social services; pressures to assimilate; the particular tribulations of being restricted to refugee camps and other exclusionary spaces; and challenges encountered in educational contexts.  The intent, then, is twofold: to interrogate discourses, processes, and structures that dehumanize immigrants, and to grapple with alternative conceptions of citizenship and belonging as well as the possibilities for legal and societal transformation that they offer at multiple levels.  Offered: periodically.

subject: Public Affairs
description: In this seminar, we will critically read and discuss the literature that frames the foundational theory and practice of sustainability across the environmental, economic, and social equity dimensions. We will examine how local governments and local organizations interact with each other and with actors at different geographic and governmental scales. Readings will include some classics of sustainability as well as important primary sources.  Cross-listed with ENVI 481B.  Offered: spring only.

subject: Public Affairs
description: Building on SUST 500, students in this class will continue to examine coupled human-nature systems; this time with a focus on policymaking and designing improvements in the systems.  Students will examine regional and global topics through the lens of communities and ways that policies and actions can influence local livability and can impact the environment at scales from local to global. The class includes as part of its investigation the environmental justice and economic implications of policies.

subject: Public Affairs
description: This seminar reviews approached to environmental decision making through the comparison of traditional and innovative approaches, including standards, taxes and tradable permits related to the formation of environmental and resource policy.  Global as well as domestic environmental issues, environmental justice and sustainable development concerns will be discussed along with the primary policy issues affecting major U.S. environmental laws.  During the course, each student will be assigned a topic or requested to select a topic for class discussion.  Cross-listed with ENVI 481T. Offered: periodically.

subject: Nursing
course_name: Cncpt H/A Nrs Adv Clin Pract
description:
NURS 502 Concepts in Health Assessment for Nurses in Advanced Clinical Practice
This course prepares the learner to assess the biopsychosocial health status of clients by obtaining a comprehensive health history and performing a thorough physical examination. Using a developmental approach, content will be presented that helps the learner differentiate between normal and abnormal findings. Methods of documentation emphasizing a nursing problem-oriented approach will be discussed. The assumption is made that the learner possesses interviewing skills and knowledge of basic anatomy and physiology. The laboratory component stresses the development of necessary assessment skills through practice with colleagues and/or clients.   

Prerequisite: RN licensure.  , (Didactic 2 credit, Practicum 1 credit).  Fall semester.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description:
Nursing 503, Scientific Inquiry:  Theoretical Foundations:
This course is an introduction to theoretical thinking in nursing. Methods of inquiry will be presented which are necessary for the development and expansion of the scientific body of knowledge in nursing. The class will include an overview of important issues in the philosophy of science, including ways of learning and patterns and sources of knowledge. Relationships among philosophy, values, science, theory, and research, and their effect on the structure of nursing knowledge will be discussed. Conceptual models and theories will be examined. In addition, theory in relation to the research process and as a basis for nursing practice will be explored. Students will acquaint themselves with the creation, process, and advancement of nursing theory.
Offered fall and spring. Prerequisite: NURS 600, can be taken concurrently. NOTE: Students cannot register for N.503 concurrently with N.535 unless instructor permission is granted.  (2- Didactic.)

subject: Nursing
description:
Distance Learning with one on-campus meeting.  The student will attend one on-campus lab experience for a competency exam and to complete the simulated breast activity.

NURS 504 offers student an opportunity to review and refresh their advanced health assessment skills.  This refresher course will be beneficial towards preparing students for entry into advanced practice clinical sites, which demand proficiency in conducting comprehensive health histories and physical examinations.  The course is designed for those students who completed Concepts in Health Assessment for Nurses in Advanced Clinical Practice more than 12 months prior or who may have previously taken an advanced health assessment course that did not provide across the lifespan content.  Students may register for 1- based on faculty advisement after careful review of academic history.

subject: Nursing
description: NURS 508 is an introductory course to the field of palliative care. Core competencies of palliative care and associated domains of clinical practice across the lifespan will be discussed and threaded throughout the curriculum. The dynamic nature of palliative care as a relatively new medical specialty will be highlighted. Emphasis on the interprofessional aspects of palliative care and hospice will be stressed, as well as the differentiation of these two closely-related disciplines. Content will provide a foundation in the philosophical and conceptual underpinnings of palliative care, for advanced nursing practice in the role of palliative care educator, nurse researcher, clinician or administrator, across all health care settings. Concepts related to advanced chronic illness management, health care systems, continuity of care, patient rights at end of life, and the provision of ?a good death? will be examined in depth. The course is based upon the Essentials of Master?s Education for Advanced Practice Nursing, the eight domains of the National Consensus Project 2018 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Quality Palliative Care, and the National Organization of Nurse Practitioner Faculties? Core Competencies.  3 credit Didactic. Summer only

subject: Nursing
description:
“This course is designed to provide the student with a foundation in theoretical and empirical knowledge from which to guide advanced nursing practice for community based clients across the age continuum from young adulthood to old age. Health assessment skills developed in NURS 502 are expanded with the introduction of evaluative tools used in comprehensive adult and geriatric assessment. Emphasis will be placed on health promotion, health prevention and maintenance of function and quality of life in the context of the normal aging process. Psychological, physiological, sociological, cultural, and developmental issues of normal aging will be examined through a life course perspective.  Consideration of health behaviors will be guided by national health objectives and health promotion/wellness models. Availability, accessibility, and economic feasibility of health care resources will be addressed.    Exploration of multidisciplinary research findings will be integrated into classroom and clinical experiences. The clinical portion of this course requires approximately 4 hours per week for a total of 60 hours in the practice setting.  The course is designed to promote professional and interprofessional interactions and cooperative learning through activities and assignments shared with students from other care disciplines. 
Prerequisites: NURS 502, NURS 518 & NURS 600; Corequisite: NURS 519 & NURS 514 (NP); or NURS 519 & NURS 556 (EDUC); or NURS 519 & NURS 550 (CNS). 3 credit (Didactic 2 credit, Practicum ) Spring semester.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description:
“This course is designed to develop the advanced practice nursing student’s knowledge, clinical assessment skill and ability to process information critical to the holistic primary care management of individuals with chronic illness across the age continuum from young adulthood to old age. Management is coordinated with client support from families, communities, and health care systems.  Potential impacts of socio-cultural, ethnic and religious considerations on client ability to manage chronic illness are examined from a life course perspective. Theories of chronic illness are discussed. Special emphasis is placed on common geriatric syndromes and the utilization of comprehensive geriatric assessment and interdisciplinary management as it relates to the older adult client’s functional status.  Current multidisciplinary research findings are applied in both classroom and clinical experiences. The clinical portion of this course requires approximately 4 hours per week for a total of 60 hours in the practice setting. Students may use the same site for both the role and clinical courses.
Prerequisite: NURS 511 & NURS 514 (NP); or NURS 511 & NURS 556 (EDUC); or NURS 511 & NURS 550 (CNS).   (Didactic 2 credit, Practicum 1 credit).  Offered fall semesters only   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description:
“This course prepares the advance practice nursing student to manage clients with complex healthcare problems as they age across the continuum from late adulthood.  Emphasis is focused   on the treatment of illnesses and geriatric syndromes associated with declining functional status in the frail elder.  Application of theories of aging, assessment skills, critical thinking and evidence based practice guidelines will drive treatment and evaluation of older adults with complex healthcare issues in community and long term care settings. Potential impacts of socio-cultural, ethnic and religious considerations on end of life health care decisions are examined from a life course perspective. Health care policy in long term care settings is examined.  The clinical portion of this course requires approximately 8 hours per week for a total of 120 hours in the practice setting. Students may use the same site for both the role and clinical courses.
Prerequisite: NURS 512 & NURS 554 (NP); or NURS 512 & NURS 551 (EDUC); or NURS 512 & NURS 557 (CNS).   (Didactic 1 credit, Practicum 2 credit).  Offered spring semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: “This is the first of three role courses enabling students to socialize into the role of the Adult-Gerontology nurse practitioner.  Class content will address the direct care provider role of the nurse practitioner in relation to the evaluation and management of health and illness care of the young adult (including late adolescents and emancipated minors), adults, and older adults (including young-old, and old-old adults).  Health education methodologies and counseling strategies pertinent to primary care practice will be explored and intervention skills developed.  Application of nursing theory in supervised clinical practice will be included and emphasized.  The focus of the adult-gerontology primary care NP is to provide patient-centered quality care to the adult and older adult population.  The adult-gerontology primary care NP applies evidence in practice designed to improve quality of care and health outcomes.  Prerequisite: NURS 502 and NURS 518.  Co-requisite: NURS 511 and NURS 519.    (Didactic 2 credit, Practicum 2 credit).  Spring semester only   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: The first of three functional role courses enables students to socialize into the role of the nurse practitioner. Class content will address the direct care provider role of the nurse practitioner in relation to the evaluation and management of health and illness care of the young and expanding family. Intervention skills for the educator and counselor roles pertinent to primary care practice will be explored. Direct preceptor supervised clinical practice provided. Prerequisite: NURS 502, NURS 518 NURS 600. Corequisites: NURS 519 and NURS 541.   (Didactic 2 credit, Practicum 2 credit). Spring semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: This is the second of three role courses enabling students to socialize into the role of nurse practitioner.  Class content addresses nursing strategies and management for family dynamics and health as they pertain to aging and contracting families.  Building on the direct care provider, counselor, and educator roles studies in the second semester; students incorporate into the nurse practitioner role the functions of consultant and researcher.  Specific individual health needs as well as the evaluation and management of common acute and chronic health problems of aging and contracting families are discussed.  Supervised clinical practice to assist students in applying theory and evidence based practice to the nursing management of these families is emphasized. Prerequisite: NURS 515 & NURS 541 Corequisite: NURS 542 (NP Only).  (Didactic 2 credit, Practicum 2 credit).  Fall semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: The last of three functional role courses enables students to socialize into the role of nurse practitioner, which includes the six components of clinician, counselor, educator, consultant, administrator, and researcher. Class content addresses both the implementation and synthesis of role components in relation to clinical decision-making and management, professional advocacy, practice models, entrepreneurial strategies, career development, and collaborative relationships. Direct preceptor supervised clinical practice provided.  Prerequisite: NURS 516 & NURS 542.  Corequisite: NURS 543.  (Didactic 2 credit. Practicum 2 credit.) Spring semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: This course explores the pathophysiologic mechanisms of disease relevant to advanced nursing practice. A systems approach is used to examine alterations in the structure and function of the human body at the molecular, cellular, tissue, organ, and body systems levels that are associated with diseases/conditions commonly encountered in primary care. Emphasis is placed on understanding the etiology of altered health states, correlating clinical and laboratory manifestations to underlying physiologic processes and pathophysiologic mechanisms, and developing advanced diagnostic and clinical reasoning skills. Consideration is also given to the psychological, social, and cultural factors that influence the health of individuals, families, and cultural groups.   Pre-requisites: None; Co-requisites: N.502   Fall semester only.

subject: Nursing
description:
Nursing 519 provides an in-depth exploration of the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of medications as well as the pharmacotherapeutic management of disease processes commonly encountered in the primary care setting. Building on skills learned in Advanced Health Assessment and Advanced Pathophysiology and supporting concurrent and subsequent functional role courses, this course assists the learner in synthesizing knowledge of patient assessment and diagnosis with pharmacological agents and treatment modalities. Emphasis is placed on developing critical thinking skills, sound clinical reasoning, and an informed decision-making approach to the pharmacological management aspects of patient care. In addition, the course offers students an opportunity to advance in their roles as expert educators and clinicians. Relevant ethical, legal, and professional practice issues as well as economic considerations are discussed throughout the course. Lifespan and developmental, race and cultural, and genetic and behavioral aspects are also significantly interwoven. The overall goal of the course is to provide the student with the fundamental knowledge and essential decision-making skills that the advanced practice nurse must have for safe and effective pharmacologic management of patients in clinical practice.
Prerequisite: NURS 502 & NURS 518.    Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: NURS 520: This course is designed for non-APRN graduate nursing student (Nurse Educator and Nurse Administrator).  Advanced Pathophysiology and Pharmacology Across the Lifespan for the non-APRN student explores concepts from pathophysiologic mechanisms of disease as well as pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of medications used to treat disease.  A systems approach is used to examine alterations in the structure and function of the human body that are associated with diseases/conditions,  Emphasis is placed on correlating clinical and laboratory manifestations to underlying physiologic or pathophysiologic mechanisms, and making application to pharmacologic modes of treatment.  Consideration is also given to the psychological, social and cultural factors that influence the health of individuals, families and cultural groups.  This course is not applicable for students seeking APRN licensure.

subject: Nursing
description: “The first course in the Family sequence, addresses health promotion of the family unit through application of family and nursing theories as well as a variety of models and frameworks related to advanced nursing practice.  Theory application is explored through case analyses.  This course focuses on the emerging, developing and expanding family.  The course is designed to promote professional and inter-professional interactions and cooperative learning.  It is based on the assumption that family health is a complex process and knowledge about family health is continually evolving.  This course has a particular emphasis on communication skills and the approach to the patient with a psychosocial complaint.  Reflective practice is introduced as a tool for personal and professional growth.  Intervention strategies discussed in the course will be utilized to create and evaluate family-based care plans in relation to the standards for advanced clinical practice.  Direct, preceptor-supervised clinical practice provided.  The course is designed to promote professional and interprofessional interactions and cooperative learning through activities and assignments shared with students from other health care disciplines.  Prerequisites:  NURS 502, NURS 518 & NURS 600.  Co-requisites: NURS 519 & NURS 553 (NP) or NURS 519 & NURS 556 (EDUC).   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 1 credit)  Spring semester only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description:
Second clinical course in the family nursing sequence addresses family, psychosocial and nursing theories appropriate for intervening with families facing the challenges of midlife.  Transitions and crises, coping strategies and the lived experience of having and managing chronic illness are explored as an avenue for understanding the dynamics, health needs and patterns of family systems. Theory application related to chronic illness is explored in greater depth through case analysis.  Assessment and advanced nursing intervention strategies for families in midlife are integrated throughout the semester. Learners apply theory-based strategies in the classroom that allow them to intervene with midlife and aging families experiencing chronic illness, in the clinical setting. This course has a special emphasis on cultural competence in the setting of advanced practice nursing. Reflective practice is utilized as a tool for personal and professional growth. Direct, preceptor-supervised clinical practice provided. This course is restricted to MS FNP Students.  
Prerequisites: NURS 519, NURS 521 and NURS 533 (NP Only)  
Note:   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
course_name: Nurs & Comm Hlth Care Delv Sys
description:
“This course focuses on healthcare systems within communities in the United States, their historical development, the major forces shaping the present status, and emerging directions. Components as well as analytic models of formal and informal healthcare delivery systems will be examined. Geographic, socio-cultural, and environmental stresses to the community and their healthcare systems will be discussed. Current healthcare reform issues, including methods of financing healthcare and issues specific to the rural community will be analyzed. Throughout the course, the implications for nursing roles and actions within healthcare organizations, and the planning, policy formulation, and evolving methods of delivering services to clients will be highlighted. How national, state, and local influences, and processes of organizational change affect the individual, small groups, and the nursing profession will be explored. Appropriate for students in MASS or MPA healthcare concentrations with permission of instructor. 
This course will be taught using an online asynchronous format.   
Offered Fall and Spring semesters.  
NOTE: FNP & A/G Students registered for the Fall: will be preassigned to attend one Inter-Professional Education (IPE) event working with Social Work, Pharmacy and Public Health students to take place one one of two dates: TBA

subject: Nursing
description:
This course is the third in the Scientific Inquiry sequence. It builds upon knowledge gained in Scientific Inquiry: Research Methods, as well as Scientific Inquiry: Theory, and focuses on application of knowledge in nursing research. Learning will be directed in four main areas: critique and analysis of completed research in nursing, generating small grant proposals for external funding, the use of the computer in data management and statistical analysis. 
Prerequisites:  NURS 600 and NURS 503 or NURS 601.  Fall semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: This course introduces principles and methods of epidemiological investigations for both infectious and non-infectious diseases. Methods that outline how the distribution and dynamic behavior of health, illness, and disease in the population contribute to an understanding of etiologic factors, modes of transmission, and pathogenesis of disease are illustrated. Both acute and chronic disease methods of epidemiologic investigation are explored. Topics to be covered include: evaluation of screening surveys, cross sectional, case control, and incidence or cohort studies; pitfalls found in epidemiologic studies; as well as statistical tests, and the selection of analytical tools to fit specific data. Predictable client populations at risk will be discussed. Students will have the opportunity to apply theory and practice with simulated and/or real data sets for analysis, and to develop their own epidemiologic investigation. Required for community health nursing students.  Fall semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: This course is the first in the sequence of Community Health Practice specialty courses.  This course is designed to place the nature and scope of community health nursing within the framework of nursing theory, nursing process, family theory, and public health principles. Models of health and health behavior are discussed. The family as client is the focus of this course. Families are assessed for health problems, stressors and strengths. Management of families with multiple health problems is the focus of clinical practice.  Intervention strategies discussed in the course are utilized while conducting family visits, evaluating the family plan of care in relation to the standards for advanced clinical practice. Rural and urban issues are addressed.  Prerequisite: NURS 502, NURS 518, NURS 540 and NURS 600.  (Didactic 2 credit, Practicum 1 credit).  Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description:
The second course in the Community Health sequence focuses on advanced community health nursing care of the community as client. Students collaborate with community people/agencies to assess major health needs; identify aggregate groups at risk; and begin to plan primary, secondary or tertiary prevention programs. Community Health Nurse Educator and Administrator students will conduct their practice in community agencies; however the Community Health Nurse Practitioner students will conduct their assessment of patient needs out of their primary care placements and will be giving direct care to patients in their clinical practice sites while collecting data on the needs of their client populations.    
Prerequisite: NURS 515 & NURS 541 (NP) or NURS 541 & NURS 556 (EDUC).  , (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 1 credit).  Fall semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description:
“The third clinical course continues to focus on advanced community health nursing care of community as client. Students continue collaboration with community groups and agencies to implement and evaluate primary, secondary or tertiary prevention programs. Advanced community health nursing role, practice, research issues are evaluated. Community Health Nurse Educators and Administrators will conduct their practice in community agencies and will develop, implement and evaluated their projects within their assigned agencies. However the Community Health Nurse Practitioner students will design, implement and evaluate their project within their assigned primary care practice while continuing to give direct care to patients in their clinical practice sites. 
Prerequisite: NURS 516 & NURS 542 (NP) or N.542 & NURS 557 (EDUC).   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 1 credit).  Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: Web-based course providing the community health nurse with essential knowledge for responding to emerging public-health threats. Emphasis is on emerging biological threats and super bugs. The role of new technologies, specifically the geographic information system (GIS), in the prevention, surveillance and control of emerging public-health threats, is also explored. Students perform a disaster risk assessment within a community and identify areas for public/community health response.  Fall semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: Web-based course that prepares the community health nurse to take a leadership role in community disaster preparedness and disaster management. The nature of disasters, their effect on the health of people and communities, and the implications for public health are appraised in relation to the role that community health nurses have in planning for and responding to natural, man-made and Na-Tech disasters. Particular emphasis is on the identification of vulnerable and at-risk populations, the coordination of resources and agency responses, the management of emergency shelters and community intervention for recovery. Students formulate a community disaster plan in response to a selected natural, man-made or Na-Tech disaster.  Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description:
The design of this course is to provide an overview of the key concepts in the field of organizational behavior. The concepts presented will include leadership, motivation, group behavior, work environment, power and influence, cultural diversity, organizational design and organizational change. The course begins with in-depth review of these concepts in theory and then provides the student with an opportunity to apply the concepts to practice in health care and public administration. The course will concentrate on healthcare organization but is applicable to a wide range of non-for profit and for profit organizations. Students will study the theory and practices of how information regarding organizational behavior is gathered and used to provide meaningful conclusions and establish the opportunity for positive organizational behavioral change. Leaders and future leaders of health delivery organizations and other public institutions will benefit from an enhanced understanding of the key concepts of organizational behavior. This course will challenge the students to analyze their own motivations and behavior, and their relationships to others and to systems as a whole.  
  Fall & Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: This course will focus the community health response to the possible use of chemical and radiological weapons of mass destruction (WMD). Course content will include disaster response to chemical and radiation incidents. Students will learn to assess the appropriate level of response to different types of chemical disasters. Students will identify the different effects of radiation, as well as the treatment required. During the course the students will be required to respond to a simulated Hazmat incident and a simulated chemical spill. This course, along with NURS 540, NURS 546, and NURS 547 lead to a certificate in Community Disaster Preparedness. Spring semester only.

subject: Nursing
description:
Nursing 550 is the first in a three semester sequence of courses designed to prepare the graduate nursing student for the clinical specialist role (CNS) in adult-gerontology nursing in diverse healthcare settings.  The CNS role is structured with seven sub-roles including:  direct care provision, consultation, systems of leadership, collaboration, coaching, research and ethical decision making, moral agency and advocacy.  Theory related to Advanced Practice Nursing will be examined to facilitate integration of these sub-roles. This course specifically concentrates on the scope and responsibilities inherent in the direct care provider, collaborator and coaching roles.
Clinical practice opportunities allow for application of knowledge and socialization to these roles. The clinical portion of this course requires 4 hours per week for a total of 60 hours in the practice setting.
Prerequisite: NURS 502, NURS 518, & NURS 600.  Corequisite: NURS 511 & NURS 519.  4 credit (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description:
Nursing 551 is the second in a three semester sequence of courses designed to prepare the graduate nursing student for the clinical specialist role (CNS) in adult-gerontology health nursing in diverse health care settings. This course specifically concentrates on the scope and responsibilities inherent in the direct care provider, consultant and systems of leadership sub-roles. Students will examine theoretical knowledge, apply clinical judgment and develop practice skills needed to improve patient outcomes and improve health care delivery from a consultant and leadership perspective
Students will practice in the CNS role in a setting appropriate for their area of interest. Clinical practice opportunities allow for application of knowledge and socialization to these roles. The clinical portion of this course requires 4 hours per week for a total of 60 hours in the practice setting.
Prerequisite: NURS 511 & NURS 550 (AG), Corequisite: NURS 512.   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Fall only.

subject: Nursing
description: The last course in the three semester sequence of courses for the CNS, focuses on the consultant and researcher components of the CNS role. These include direct care provider/case manager, counselor, educator, consultant, leader, and researcher. Clinical practice opportunities allow for application of theories pertinent to the role. Direct preceptor supervised clinical practice provided. Clinical practice opportunities allow for application of knowledge and socialization to these roles. The clinical portion of this course requires 8 hours per week for a total of 120 hours in the practice setting.  Prerequisite: NURS 512 & NURS 551.   (Didactic: 2 credits, Practicum, 2 credits).  Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: The first of three functional role courses enables students to socialize into the role of the nurse practitioner. Class content will address the direct care provider role of the nurse practitioner in relation to the evaluation and management of health and illness care of the young and expanding family. Intervention skills for the educator and counselor roles pertinent to primary care practice will be explored. Direct preceptor supervised clinical practice provided. Prerequisite: NURS 502, NURS 518 & NURS 600. Corequisites: NURS 519 & NURS 521.   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits - 120 hours clinical).  Spring semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: This is the second of three role courses enabling students to socialize into the role of nurse practitioner.  Class content addresses nursing strategies and management for family dynamics and health as they pertain to aging and contracting families.  Building on the direct care provider, counselor, and educator roles studies in the second semester; students incorporate into the nurse practitioner role the functions of consultant and researcher.  Specific individual health needs as well as the evaluation and management of common acute and chronic health problems of aging and contracting families are discussed.  Supervised clinical practice to assist students in applying theory and evidence based practice to the nursing management of these families is emphasized. Prerequisite: NURS  521 & NURS 553 (FNP) or NURS 511 & NURS 514 (AG).  Corequisite: NURS 522 (FNP) or NURS 512 (AG).   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum  - 120 hours clinical).  Fall semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: The last of three functional role courses enables students to socialize into the role of nurse practitioner, which includes the six components of clinician, counselor, educator, consultant, administrator, and researcher. Class content addresses both the implementation and synthesis of role components in relation to clinical decision-making and management, professional advocacy, practice models, entrepreneurial strategies, career development, and collaborative relationships. Direct preceptor supervised clinical practice provided. Prerequisite: NURS 522 & 554 (FNP) or NURS 512 & NURS 554 (AG).  Corequisite: NURS 596 (FNP) or NURS 513 (AG).   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits - 120 hours clinical).  Spring semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides the philosophical foundations of education, scholarly teaching and discourse. Content addresses the goals of education, human development, behavioral, cognitive, social and constructivist learning theories, multiple intelligences and the physiology of the brain in relation to learning. Philosophies of education; ways of knowing and thinking; the nature of learning; learning styles; intellectual development; cultural determinants of learning and recent theories about learning will be explored. Curricular models, curricular planning and contemporary curriculum development paradigms in higher education and nursing education will be discussed. Prerequisites: NURS 502, NURS 518 & NURS 600.   (Didactic , Practicum 1 credit).  Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: “The course focuses on the design and development of courses, curricula and instruction in nursing education and the relationship between learning theory, learning, teaching, and evaluation in nursing education. Content includes the discussion and analysis of formal and tacit knowledge; classification/taxonomies of learning (cognitive, affective, social and psychomotor) requisite to developing objectives/outcomes. Particular emphasis is given to the implications of ethnicity, culture, gender, and rurality on teaching and learning in order to prepare culturally competent teachers and practitioners. Clinical hours will be spent with faculty master teachers/preceptors developing and analyzing objectives, analyzing teaching strategies, teaching undergraduate nursing students, developing problem-based scenarios, guiding online discussion groups and observation, and analysis of evaluation of learning. Prerequisite: NURS 521 & NURS 556 (FNP) or NURS 511 & NURS 556 (AG) or NURS 541 & NURS 556 (CH) or NURS 556 & NURS 565 (FPMHNP); Corequisite: NURS 522 (FNP) or NURS 512 (AG) or NURS 542 (CH) or (NURS 563 (FPMHNP).   (Didactic , Practicum 1 credit).  Fall semesters.

subject: Nursing
course_name: Info & Ed Tech In Nursing Educ
description:
This course prepares nursing faculty with the knowledge and skills related to information and educational technology to promote student learning. Critical evaluation of multimedia and technology in meeting the needs of diverse student populations is explored. Students use computer applications to produce multimedia instructional materials and for course management. Emphasis is placed on application and modeling of sound pedagogical principles and research-based practices. Ethical standards, intellectual property and copyright laws are addressed and applied. NOTE: This course is the 4th in the series only required of those students completing the Advanced Certificate in Nursing Education. Prerequisites:  NURS 556.  Corequisite: NURS 557 (FNP only by permission of instructor).
 (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Fall semesters

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides advanced knowledge of psychotropic medications in current practice. Content includes the indications, targeted effects, interactions, side effects and potential adverse effects of psychotropics including antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, mood stabilizing agents, and anxiolytics. Prerequisite: NURS 519. Note: Psychopharmacology taken for two (2) credits is a required course for graduate nursing students whose clinical specialization is in Family Psychiatric Mental Health.  Other graduate nursing students may enroll to take the course as a two (2) or three (3) credit nursing elective.  Fall and summer semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: In this course, students explore attitudes about mental health with a focus on, crisis intervention and prevention and management of acute psychiatric conditions in pediatric and adult  populations. Students address disorder  including anxiety disorders, obsessive compulsive disorders, trauma/stress related disorders, dissociative disorders, personality disorders, child /adolescent disorders, sexual disorders, and issues related to violence. Prerequisite: NURS 562 & 565.   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Fall semesters.

subject: Nursing
description:
“NURS 564 - PMH Spec II: Chronic Illnesses
This course focuses on the assessment and management of complex, serious and persistent psychiatric and co-occurring disorders across the lifespan. The role of the FPMH NP in assessing, diagnosing and managing chronic conditions such as psychotic disorders, mood disorders, substance dependence, cognitive disorders, HIV and AIDS, and co-occurring physical and psychiatric disorders in diverse individuals is emphasized. Leadership and advocacy roles of the FPMH NP as an agent of healthcare policy change are stressed. Prerequisite: NURS 562 & NURS 565.   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).   Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: This foundational course introduces students to the multiple roles of the PMH NP. Competencies and scope of care of the PMH NP are addressed. Ethical and legal issues related to advance practice psychiatric nursing are emphasized, as are the theoretical foundations of advanced psychiatric mental health nursing. Through class and clinical experiences, students acquire necessary methods and skills for completing comprehensive mental health assessments for culturally diverse individuals of all ages, utilize pertinent diagnostic testing, develop differential and definitive diagnoses, and develop health promotion plans. Prerequisite:  NURS 502 & NURS 518.  Corequisite: NURS 519.   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description:
Research evidence for best practices in individual therapy provides the basis for exploration of intervention models meeting the needs of clients across all age spans and cultural groups. Content includes solution focused/cognitive behavioral, developmental/psychodynamic, existential/humanistic, and trauma processing models, as well as common factors used by effective therapists across all intervention approaches. Course includes ongoing self evaluation as integral to professional development in the therapist role. Prerequisite: NURS 563 & NURS 565.   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Fall semesters.  
**Please Note: Course fee applies.  Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description:
NURS 567 - PMHNP Role III Fam/Grp PsyTher
This course builds on the skills acquired in previous courses and provides the basis for understanding and implementing family therapy and group therapy. Current theories and models of family therapy and group therapy are explored with an emphasis on process and dynamics. Considerations and challenges in providing psychotherapy to culturally diverse families and groups are explored and discussed. Prerequisite: NURS 563 or NURS 564 and 566.   (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Spring semester.

subject: Nursing
course_name: ADD Care Mgmt for Rur&Vuln Pop
description: This course will provide graduate nurse practice students knowledge related to the current opioid epidemic and its effects on the rural population. A key concept explored in this course is that many people with opioid addictions also have severe and persistent mental health concerns. There is a lack of treatment and resources for both opioid and mental health issues and this course will explore treatment options, ways to increase engagement with patients and their families, significant others, and communities, as well as a focus on prevention in children, teens, and adults in the community. The following topics will be explored in this course: principles of prescribing medications for opioid use disorder with consideration of special populations including pregnant women, adolescents, and older adults, harm reduction, and other therapeutic modalities for this special population.

subject: Nursing
description: Students will explore current issues and concerns in nursing and the delivery of healthcare as they transition to the advanced practice role. Class discussions will focus on present and future problems facing the profession, intra and inter professional relationships and socio-political forces influencing the delivery of healthcare. Legislative and other potential solutions to issues raised will be addressed. The role of the master’s prepared nurses in social, political, legal, ethical, and policy issues will be discussed. Responsibility of advanced practice nurses to their own professional development and career trajectory will also be explored. Prerequisite: Role I and II across all specializations. Corequisite: Role III across all specializations.   Spring only.

subject: Nursing
description:
This course is designed to assist the advanced practice nurse in gaining the necessary knowledge, skills and attitudes needed to provide care in using telehealth technology, to provide healthcare to rural and vulnerable populations.  Throughout the course, we will examine the different technologies available that can foster clinical practice and outreach to patient populations.  All students will have the opportunity to engage in simulation experiences using different types of telehealth technologies as a means of preparing themselves for future practice.
N.502 is a required pre-requisite to this course.

subject: Nursing
description:
This course examines application of evidence-based practice to clinical laboratory methods and imaging modalities with a primary objective to develop diagnostic evaluation by exploring the equipment and techniques, potential risks, and clinical utility of various laboratory methods and imaging modalities. This course is designed to enhance the clinical decision-making skills for advanced nursing practice.
Clinical Reasoning lies at the heart of formulating diagnoses, deciding what tests to order and selected treatments. To assist in the clinical decision making process , this course will also examine and explore how we think, and what influences our thinking. We will examine the causes of diagnostic error and ways to avoid these pitfalls.  
Since the course provides a foundation for clinical practice, part of the learning experience will involve a clinical component that includes the student?s participation in diagnostic testing areas.
Prerequisite: NURS 502, NURS 518, NURS 519 and 610.    DI LEARN. Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: NURS 581B - Forensic Health Essentials This course provides an overview of various forensic disciplines, as well as forensic assessment, the collection and preservation of evidence, criminal aspects of forensics, death investigation, crime analysis, crime prevention, basic civil issues, such as malpractice, child custody, elder law and personal injury, promoting one’s practice, and the differences between collaboration and consultation. This course is online asynchronous. 3 cr. Spring & Summer semester.

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides an overview of forensic and medicolegal issues as they relate to the investigation of an individual’s death. Content includes how deaths are investigated in the United States, postmortem changes, common injury patterns and findings, cause and manner of death, special types of death investigations, and working with families. Dr. Lunn is a medical investigator and criminologist in the Denver metro area with extensive experience in the investigation of violent and high profile deaths having been an invited speaker at local, state and national trainings. In service to the profession, Dr. Lunn is the former Vice President of the American Board of Medicolegal Death Investigators, a committee member for the National Association of Medical Examiners, and a committee member for a NIJ scientific working group.     Spring and Summer sessions.

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides an overview of forensic health issues as they relate to perpetrators of violent crimes, including intrafamilial violence, sexual violence, stalking, workplace violence, and homicide. Content also includes forensic roles, crime classifications, wrongful convictions, relationship between animal cruelty and human violence, offender needs and rights, juvenile offenders, and correctional health. Students also receive an introduction to criminal profiling.    Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides an overview of forensic health issues as they relate to victims of violent crimes, such as intrafamilial violence, sexual violence, stalking, workplace violence, homicide, and other issues. Content includes responding to victim responses to trauma; victim’s resources; victimization of children, women, men, elders and persons with disabilities; and expert witness testimony.  Fall semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: Courses under this section will be offered based on availability of instructor and request of students. This course explores the intricacies of forensic pediatrics where children and adolescents are victims and/or offenders of violence. Topics include: the effects of violence on youth, interviewing and assessing children/adolescents, evidence, expert witness testimony, compassion fatigue & vicarious victimization, children of incarcerated parents, child abuse, shaken baby syndrome, fictitious disorder imposed on others, sexual assault and exploitation, the juvenile justice system, delinquency, child delinquents, female delinquents, animal cruelty, arson, gangs, bullying, and child death investigation. Graduate students will also choose from Pediatric Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner, School Violence or Sudden Unexpected Infant Death Investigator modules.  Fall semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: Courses under this section will be offered based on availability of instructor and request of students. Nursing 581K Mental Health and Aging in the 21st Century  Description: This course will give a broad overview of mental health and aging in the United States. The course will discuss the current demographic of the older population and their current mental health needs. The biological, psychosocial and social theories of aging and mental health will be examined. Common psychiatric disorders in the older population will be presented. The challenges to meeting the needs of the aging population will be explored including access to care, cost and legality. Note: This is an asyncronous online course for graduate students.  Summer or Winter session, based on faculty availability.

subject: Nursing
description: The over all design of this course is to introduce financial management concepts to the non-financial manager.  The course will concentrate on healthcare organizations but is applicable to a wide range of organizations.  This course will introduce the topics of financial and managerial accounting and finance as they apply to the provision of health care services. Students will study the theory and practice of how financial information is gathered and used to provide meaningful conclusions about the financial position and performance of health care organizations. Leaders and future leaders of health delivery organizations including hospitals, clinical practices, health insurance providers and other not-for-profit organizations will benefit from an enhanced understanding of key financial and policy issues. This course will provide the learner with the knowledge necessary to be able to deal with these financial issues.  Summer session.

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides a practical examination of sexual offending and victimization. While it is open to all graduate students, it is designed for students who may work with these populations during their careers. Modules are: Underlying Framework; Types of Sexual Assault; Sexual Exploitation and Human Trafficking; Victim Populations & the Effects of Sexual Assault on Victims; Evaluation of Sexual Assault Victims; Interventions for Sexual Assault Victims; Perpetrators of Sexual Violence; Offender Populations; Offender Assessment; Treatment and Supervision of Sex Offenders; and Prevention of Sexual Violence.    Summer session.

subject: Nursing
description: Functional Role III, Nurse Educator, is designed to help students synthesize teaching and learning theory and the pedagogical approaches they have been studying in preparation for the nursing faculty role. This course is the practical application of theory and scholarship to current and emerging challenges facing the nursing profession and faculty in teaching. The course provides the student with direct, real life experience in preparation for assuming the role of a faculty member within a School of Nursing and provides the opportunity for students to implement their personal philosophy of teaching and learning. Content includes trends and issues in nursing, higher education, and the complexity of teaching and learning. Educational administration and college organization and the roles of Academic and Student Affairs in promoting student success will be explored. Students will engage in clinical and classroom teaching, course development, assessment and evaluation of students and will participate in school of nursing and university activities. Prerequisite: NURS 522 & 557 (FNP) or NURS 512 & NURS 557 (AG) or NURS 542 & NURS 557 (CH).  Corequisite: NURS 596 (FNP) or NURS 513 (AG) or NURS 542 (CH).    (Didactic 2 credits, Practicum 2 credits).  Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description:
Application and synthesis of theory relevant to practice of family nursing with a special focus on families in later life.  Common experiences associate with aging and illness such as changes in self-image and relationships, and related APN interventions, are emphasized.  This course has an emphasis on palliative care, advance directives and having difficult conversations with patients.  Direct, preceptor-supervised clinical practice provided.  Prerequisite: NURS 522 & NURS 554 (FNP) or NURS 522 & NURS 557 (EDUC).   (Didactic 1 credit, Practicum 2 credits).  
Co-requisite of NURS 555 or NURS 590.  Spring semesters only.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Nursing
description:
In-depth study in particular area of interest, under direction of appropriate faculty. Consent of coordinator of graduate program required. May be taken more than once.  Offered fall, spring and summer sessions with permission of instructor or Graduate Program Director.   
** Please Note: When an Independent Study includes a clinical component: Course fees apply.  Refer to the Schedule of Classes

subject: Nursing
description:
In-depth study in particular area of interest, under direction of appropriate faculty. Consent of coordinator of graduate program required. May be taken more than once. This is a NON-clinical Independent Study course.

Fall, spring and summer semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: Research findings influence nursing practice, theory and education and contribute to the body of nursing science. Understanding the various ways in which research is conducted and being able to critique research and apply findings to nursing practice are essential skills for advanced practice nurses. This course is designed to provide fundamental methodological and statistical skills needed by nurses.  It covers the research process from conceptualization to the statistical analysis and interpretation of findings. The emphasis of the course is on the selection and application of appropriate research designs and statistical procedures.    Fall and Spring semesters

subject: Nursing
description: The course will examine different epistemologies and their impact on current approaches to nursing research, theory development, and clinical practice.  Participants will examine the writings of selected nursing theorists as well as theorists from affiliated disciplines relevant to their field of practice.  The course will examine what does understanding or knowing mean and what is the nature of scientific practice.  Fundamental elements central to theory, research, and practice will be presented with opportunities for application and practice. Participants will study the development of middle range theories to guide practice and research within the metaparadigm of nursing. In addition, the philosophical, ethical, and historical issues inherent in the development of science provide the base advanced nursing practice.  This is a MS level course.    Fall semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: Course content will include experience in conceptualizing clinical nursing phenomena as an initial step in performing nursing research.  Psychological, cognitive, social and ethical dimensions of selected concepts relevant to nursing practice with rural and other vulnerable populations will be examined theoretically and operationally.    Spring semesters.  Prerequisites: NURS 608 & NURS 609, or permission of instructor.  Restricted to enrollment by PhD students or by permission of instructor.

subject: Nursing
description: Advanced procedures for data analysis and statistical inference in nursing research.  Multivariate procedures included; their utility in investigation of nursing problems presented.  The ultimate goal of the course is to arm doctoral students with statistical data analysis skills needed to complete the data analysis components of their dissertations. After a review of the research process and terminology, fundamentals of SPSS will be introduced.  Each week, a new statistical technique will be discussed for its utility and application in research, followed by a hands-on SPSS sessions and SPSS assignments and exercises.  Overall, students will integrate research methodology, statistics and data analytical techniques to apply them to an analytical paper similar to a journal article.    Spring semesters.  Prerequisites: NURS 608

subject: Nursing
description:
This course provides an overview to promote your understanding of qualitative inquiry as a research methodology for the human sciences.  This course will focus on research design, methods for data collection and analysis, interpretation, and evaluation using the naturalistic paradigm and qualitative methods.  By the completion of this course, you will be competent consumers of qualitative studies with knowledge of the utility of qualitative methodologies.  Topics for discussion in the course include the historical and  philosophical development of qualitative methodologies within the human sciences and the influence of logical positivism on the development of the received view of science.  You will be introduced to different qualitative research designs and the phenomenon of interest that these designs explore.  Issues of veracity, understandability and credibility of qualitative methods will be explored and discussed.  Literature available to the qualitative researcher will be reviewed and methods for data collection, analysis, and interpretation will be introduced.  You will develop a beginning understanding of qualitative methods of inquiry and the contribution of these methods to the epistemology of nursing science.    Fall semester.  Prerequisites: NURS 602 & NURS 609, or permission of the instructor.

Note: this course is restricted to PhD Students only.

subject: Nursing
description: Course content includes measurement theory and practice for nursing and health-related research. Techniques of test and instrument construction, statistical analysis of reliability and validity, item generation, psychometric testing and major concepts of measurement will be presented. Students will critically analyze and critique a variety of instruments and complete some of the initial steps required to develop an instrument.    Spring semesters.  Prerequisites: NURS 608

subject: Nursing
description: This course is designed to assist students in developing a research proposal for the dissertation.  The intent is that, at the close of the semester, students will be ready (or almost ready) to formally defend their proposals.  The focus of the course is three-fold: 1) the identification of researchable questions that advance nursing practice and/or health policy, 2) the development of a logical outline for the previous research on your topic, and 3) the development of a feasible research project to address a selected question.  Students will work with the course instructor, their dissertation chairs, and other students in the course to develop and defend their dissertation proposal. Prerequisites: NURS 603, NURS 604 & NURS 640.  Must be in final semester of PhD program coursework to enroll.    Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description:
Research findings influence practice, theory and education and contribute to the body of science.  Understanding the various ways in which research is conducted, being able to critically analyze research findings in literature and conducting independent research are essential skills for PhD prepared nurses and other health professionals.  This course is designed to provide fundamental methodological and statistical skills needed by PhD students.  It covers the research process from conceptualization to the statistical analysis and interpretation of findings.  The emphasis of the course is on the selection and application of appropriate research designs and statistical procedures.  Furthermore, SPSS will be introduced and basic data entry and analysis procedures will be provided.  
  Fall and Spring semesters. Note: Course is restricted to PhD Students ONLY

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides participants with an opportunity to examine philosophy of science as it relates to the evolution of the discipline of nursing.  The distinction between the discipline and the profession of nursing is clarified.  The multiple paradigms of nursing with their conceptual and theoretical modes are analyzed.  There is  focus on original thinking to create unique conceptualizations from synthesizing literature and various artforms.  The interrelationships among philosophy, ethics, theory development, research and practice are analyzed as they relate to the theoretical basis of nursing.    Fall semester.  This is a PhD level course.  Pre-Co- Requisite: NURS 608

subject: Nursing
description: Students will learn to develop the requisite knowledge, skills, and attitudes for integration of evidence-based practice in the clinical setting. Students learn the steps of evidence-based practice and facilitate exploration of published research and other scientific evidence. Students will develop skills in posing a structured clinical question, searching relevant literature from a variety of databases, compiling it into a reference database, and evaluating it based on methodological criteria. These courses are specific to the DNP curriculum.  Prerequisite: NURS 600.    Fall semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: The purpose of this course is to enable Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) students to become proficient in the use of information systems/technology resources to implement quality improvement initiatives and support practice decision-making. This course draws on the body of knowledge from cognitive, computer, design, and information sciences. A systems approach will be used to examine the benefits and constraints of current infrastructure, including both hardware and software, for administrative and clinical decisions making. Using an evidence-based practice approach, the student will analyze a clinical practice information system and develop a quality improvement plan that addresses a system deficiency or expands the current capacity of a system to evaluate or monitor patient outcomes. Students will also explore a broad range of healthcare technology applications including systems for consumer health education. In addition, students will demonstrate knowledge of standards and principles for selecting and evaluating information systems and patient care technology as well as assess associated risks related to ethical, regulatory, and legal issues and propose strategies to maximize benefits and minimize potential harms.    Spring semester.

subject: Nursing
description: This course will explore rural culture using theories, frameworks and methodologies from various disciplines. Rural life will be analyzed to identify factors related to health care risks and needs.  Exploration of rural life through the humanities as well as the research literature will give the student in in-depth understanding of rural populations.    Spring semester.

subject: Nursing
description: This course will explore vulnerable populations using theories, frameworks, and methodologies from various disciplines.  The impact of vulnerability on health care will be the focus.  Exploration of vulnerable populations through the humanities as well as the research literature will give the student an in-depth understanding of vulnerable populations.    Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description:
“Course content will explore the application of theoretical concepts, constructs and models for research and practice of nursing.  Students will analyze nursing theoretical frameworks pertinent for research either directed at health promotion and disease prevention or alterations from health (primarily chronic illness).  Students will review and critique research studies including those germane to rural and/or vulnerable populations and examine issues of methodology, instrument selection and development, sampling, data collection and measurement.  Students will explore the rich variety of models and theoretical constructs existing today in preparation for integrating nursing theory in their area of research interest.  Course content will include theories and models that will guide research.  Additionally, research related to disease states, chronic illness and patient outcomes will be explored as well as prevention.  Theoretical constructs are included that are related to the individual, environment and health integrating public health, behavioral science.  Cultural aspects as well as theories and models relating to nursing science and theories of regulation will be explored.  Students will develop an in-depth review of the body of literature in relation to their research interests, using a nursing theoretical framework from either a health promotion/disease prevention model or alteration from health (chronic illness) appropriate to the literature they plan to review for their dissertation.
  Fall semesters.  Prerequisites: NURS 602, NURS 608 & NURS 609, or with permission of the instructor.

subject: Nursing
description: The goal of this course is to analyze the elements and functioning of healthcare systems of selected nations in comparison to the American healthcare system. Political, social, cultural and economic factors effecting rural and urban healthcare systems are examined from a global perspective. The strengths and weaknesses of systems are explored in relation to economics and outcomes. Role of public health politics in policy development and implementation in rural and urban areas is analyzed.   Fall semesters  Prerequisites: NURS 608 or with permission of instructor

subject: Nursing
description: The goal of this course is to analyze current major U.S. health policy issues and the critical processes and forces that shape them. The health policy issues addressed include rural health, Medicare, Medicaid, the uninsured, public health, the impact of welfare policy on healthcare, managed-care development and regulation, state and federal healthcare reform, and others. Discussions will focus on the politics of health policy in terms of legislative and executive processes at the state and federal level; key forces involved including economic, social, ethical and political factors; and central players of importance, including special-interest groups, lobbyists, the press, elected officials, legislative staff and public agencies. Specific rural health issues will be suggested by students and discussions will be led by students.   Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: This is a social science course about health disparities across populations. Students will learn to analyze and identify what it means to live in various geographic locations (national and international), and how place may influence social behavior, and affect the individual’s chance for health and survival. Sociological concepts and their potential influence beyond the individual to communities and vulnerable populations are to be synthesized in this course.  This knowledge is critical for effective healthcare practice and for health policy formation and reform for rural and vulnerable populations.  This course contextualizes the rural/urban dichotomy relative to industrialization, post-industrialization health and mortality transition.    Fall semesters.

subject: Nursing
description:
This course focuses on the students use of evidence-based clinical practice guidelines to assist in the development, implementation, and evaluation of the plan of advanced nursing care. Proficiency may be acquired through a variety of methods, including, but not limited to: attaining case management skills, completing patient or practice contact hours, demonstrating experiential clinical competencies, or a combination of these elements. These courses are specific to the DNP curriculum. Prerequisites: Completion of both specialization and role sequences (Family, Community Health, Adult-Gerontological or Family Psychiatric Mental Health tracks). Prerequisite: NURS 651.  
  Fall semester.

subject: Nursing
description:
This course is the first of three sequential courses in the DNP program. The academic focus is on the comprehensive and systematic assessment of healthcare problems the students wish to explore.  Diverse and culturally sensitive approaches are used in developing a scholarly project.  This project will identify a need for clinical advancement of health care outcomes in the practice setting. The students will complete the first two chapters of their scholarly project. Prerequisites: NURS 610 and Specialization III and Role III courses.  
 (Didactic 1 credit, Practicum 2 credits).  Spring semester only.

subject: Nursing
description:
This course is the second in a three semester sequence required of all DNP students.  It focuses on the continued development and implementation of the DNP Capstone Project.  It is expected that you will begin this course with a first draft of Chapters one and two completed.  Course activities will include: applying for and receiving IRB approval, obtaining funds for project implementation if applicable, collecting project information, and working collaboratively with clinical agencies where the projects will be implemented.  An updated review of the literature will be continued this semester; and an analysis of the project findings will begin.  It is expected that Chapters three and four will be near completion by the end of this course. Barriers and facilitators of capstone projects will be discussed.  Please reference the examples of DSON DNP Capstone Projects as a guide in writing chapters 3 and 4.  These are to be used as guides only with permission of the authors. 
Prerequisites: NURS 651.   (Didactic 1 credit, Practicum 2 credits).  Fall semester only.

subject: Nursing
description: This course is the third and culminating course for the DNP capstone project. Students will present their current project status, evaluation methodology, dissemination plans, and future recommendations in the seminar. Dissemination of the project outcomes through a publishable scholarly paper will be completed. Methods to address Healthy People 2020 objectives will be included in the evaluation of this project. Prerequisite: NURS 652.   (Didactic 1 credit, Practicum 2 credits) Spring semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: The DNP Scholarly Writing course is a foundational course for students to gain expertise in scholarly writing. Scholarly writing for professionals prepares graduate students with the knowledge and skills necessary to be competent with scholarly writing. This course prepares graduate students to successfully meet the scholarly writing demands of doctoral level writing as well as the writing standards for publication. Practical experience in the application of scholarly writing, including refining APA writing skills, and formatting clinical scholarly project documents necessary for graduate school, publication and employment success will be completed in this course. Students will complete of an analysis of their individual writing strengths and areas of need, the development of a scholarly writing portfolio and plan for continuous improvement writing which will be shared with program course instructors.

subject: Nursing

Proficiency may be acquired through a variety of methods, including, but not limited to: attaining case management skills, completing patient or practice contact hours, demonstrating experiential clinical competencies, or a combination of these elements. These courses are specific to the DNP curriculum. Prerequisite: NURS 651 (Can be taken currently with instructors permission).    Fall and spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: NURS 660 or an equivalent is required of all PhD students. The course is designed to prepare learners to teach in academic, healthcare, or continuing education settings. Topics aimed at developing competencies as an individual teacher include philosophies of education; theories of learning; student learning outcomes and assessment processes; teaching techniques and strategies; and the use of technology in instruction. Instruction will be, developing competencies that foster leadership in nursing education include curriculum design and development; creation and management of clinical experiences and placements; funding of educational programs; program evaluation; and accreditation. Students without teaching experience may elect NURS 661 to gain that experience.    Fall semesters only.

subject: Nursing
description: This course provides students with the opportunity to engage in a directed teaching experience.  The material taught and the settings are individually designed by the faculty supervisor to both meet the needs of different graduate students and also leverage their particular clinical expertise.  This course is only for those students who have had no prior teaching experience.   Fall and Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: This course is the first of two research seminars designed to assist PhD students to become active researchers and to develop research skill sets.  Both the seminars (NURS 690 & NURS 691) provide an opportunity to work with faculty in the development and applications of research skills.  You may choose to work with different faculty over the series or stay with one faculty or research team throughout the two seminars.  The first portion of this course introduces you to research conducted by faculty, requires human research ethical training, and provides a review of principals of scientific writing.    Fall semester.

subject: Nursing
description: This is the second of two research seminars designed to assist PhD students to become active researchers, and to develop research skill sets. The emphasis of NURS 691 is on improving existing research skills and the development of additional skills.  Each one of the two semesters (NURS 690 & NURS 691) allow students the opportunity to work with an individual faculty throughout the series or with a variety  of researchers for individual or team projects.  You may choose to wok with different faculty over the series or stay with one faculty or research team throughout the two seminars.     Fall or Spring semesters.

subject: Nursing
description: Independent study is a mechanism by which students can study a definitive area in depth under the direction of faculty members. Students engaged in independent study are responsible for their own learning within the guidelines of the learning contract established with the supervising faculty member. Independent study can be counted as elective credit and may–with the approval of the Director of the Graduate Program–be used in place of a regular course. Note that extenuating circumstances must be validated by the Director to accommodate a request for the use of an Independent Study in place of a normal course offering. Grading procedures for independent study are determined by the student and the faculty member and may be either normally graded or pass/fail. See full Independent Study Guidelines in the DSON Graduate Student Handbook.   Fall, spring and summer semesters.
