subject: Geology
description: Introduction to the classification, global distribution and origin of igneous and metamorphic rocks in the context of plate tectonics. Identification of pressure, temperature and compositional variables involved in petrogenesis. Examination of mineral textures and rock fabric in hand samples and thin sections. Three one-hour lectures, one three-hour laboratory per week. Prerequisites: GEOL 212/303 and 214/302, or consent of instructor. Spring,

subject: Geology
description: Characteristics and origin of sediment grains; physical, chemical and biological processes of sedimentation; diagenesis and rock classification; definition and spatial correlation of stratigraphic units; sedimentary environments and their deposits. Three hours of lectures and one three-hour laboratory or field trip per week. Prerequisites: GEOL 211/311, 212/303, and 213/301, or consent of instructor. Spring,

subject: Geology
description: This course presents an overview of the fundamentals of seismic methods, including, but not limited to active and passive source seismic techniques, gravity and magnetics. The course involves lecture and discussion sessions of multiple case studies. The course aims to provide students with a broad understanding of the current applications and future direction of applied geophysical methods.  Prerequisites:  MATH 221 or 225, PHYS 121 or 131, and GEOL 214/302, or consent of instructor.  Fall or Spring,

subject: Geology
description: Fundamental aspects of solid earth geophysics: gravity, rotational dynamics, tides; equations of state of the interior; geothermal heat flow, Earth’s thermal history; geomagnetic field. Observations and theory emphasized. Three one-hour lectures, one-hour laboratory per week. Prerequisites: MATH 371, PHYS 331 and 341

subject: Geology
description: Applications of shallow geophysical methods, such as seismic refraction and reflection, gravity, electrical resistivity and ground-penetrating radar applicable to environmental geology, hydrogeology, sedimentology, neotectonics and earthquake engineering. Field experiments, including data collection and processing on PCs or UNIX workstations, illustrate the state of the art in the determination of sub-surface structure and in situ material properties. Intended for advanced geology and environmental studies students.  Prerequisite:  GEOL 214/302 or consent of instructor.  Spring,

subject: Geology
description: This course introduces applications in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) that solve geological, anthropological, and environmental problems. The course provides introduces students to spatial analysis in these fields using commercial GIS and R based software packages. Lectures cover analytic topics and skills while the lab portion is focused on developing research projects in their area of interest. The course provides students the background necessary to develop, execute, and troubleshoot research projects that involve spatial analyses. Restriction: No Freshman. Three hours of lecture and one three-hour lab per week. Offered once a year.

subject: Geology
description: Geomicrobiology examines microbiological processes that influence earth and environmental systems. The course introduces fundamental concepts of microbial diversity, energetics and metabolisms, microbe/mineral interactions, microbial influence on environmental chemistry, biogeochemical cycles, and microorganisms as geochemical agents in the geologic record. Students are introduced to basic geomicrobiological laboratory methods. Implications of terrestrial “extremophilic” microorganisms to the evolution of terrestrial life and to the search for extraterrestrial life are also discussed. Prerequisites/corequisites: one of the following: GEOL 213/301, 366, 370/304, 470, ENV 370, BIOL 311, 314. Spring,   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

description: Sampling methods, analysis and interpretation of results acquired from collection of environmental samples. Focus is on tracing inorganic pollutants in the atmosphere and hydrosphere. subject: History
description: This course investigates the current global refugee crisis from an interdisciplinary perspective while focusing on the historical background, root causes of the crisis, and the birth of the modern refugee regime.  It also investigates the efforts and challenges associated with dealing with forced displacement with an emphasis on refugee voices and experiences.  Topics of inquiry include issues of human rights, international law, humanitarian aid, immigration, what it means to be a refugee, public health and security concerns, and efforts facilitating and hindering aid. Restricted to students enrolled in the RN-BS Online Nursing Program. Offered regularly.

subject: History
description: This course investigates United States immigration and citizenship (c. 1750-present). It looks at policies, laws, and cultures associated with citizenship, race, gender, and ethnicity in the US, how these notions have transformed over time, and how they have affected access to wealth, education, and status in order to explore the complicated, haphazard, and often-fraught experience of immigrants within the US. Major issues engaged include European, LatinX, Asian, and African immigration to the US, Native-American experiences, issues of citizenship, racism, ethnicity, inclusion and exclusion, and assimilation and integration with a focus on immigrant voices and experiences. Restricted to students enrolled in the RN-BS Online Nursing Program. Offered regularly.

subject: History
description: Development of Western ideas and institutions from beginnings of Greek civilization to Europe of 1500. Significant aspects of culture, society, politics that have shaped modern world.

subject: History
description: Western civilization traced in its development from 1500 to present time, with emphasis on Europe, Europeans and their relationships to other peoples.

subject: History
description: Covers the origins and history of the United States from before European colonization to the aftermath of the Civil War, a fascinating, violent, and powerful history, endeavoring to do justice to the people, in all their diversity, who together created the ideals, institutions, and realities that continue to shape our culture today. Subjects and issues addressed are: cross-cultural encounters; the causes and consequences of the American Revolution; economic development and transformations; the development of political institutions; changing roles for women; slavery and its connection to the causes of the Civil War; and the aftermath of civil war, especially for African Americans.

subject: History
description: Development of American civilization from the latter part of the 19th Century to the present. Agrarianism, capitalism, industrialism, racism, urbanization, immigration, colonial imperialism and world power, reform and reaction, corporate economy and corporate state, modern American expansionism.

subject: History
description: An introduction to the geographies, cultures and historical experiences of East Asia, particularly China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. In addition to overviews of each of these countries, the course will focus on topics illustrating both the unity and diversity of East Asia: perceptions of each other, of the West and by the West; the religious/ philosophical traditions of Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism; the modern histories of the four countries since 1600; the growth of interconnections between East Asia and the rest of the world; the role of imperialism in modern East Asia; the roles of nationalism, revolution, and socialism, and the future of East Asia in the twenty-first century. Offered regularly.

subject: History
description: A thematic exploration of global history in the period 1500 to the present and the ways in which societies and peoples have confronted fundamental issues of the human condition. Examines developments in China, India, Africa, the Middle East, Europe and the Americas. Themes include the impact of the European conquest of the New World; industrial transformations; subjects and citizens; revolts and revolutions, nationalisms; wars and decolonization; globalization.

subject: History
description: In this course, we examine patterns of development, change, continuity, and exchange in the premodern world. This entails an extensive survey of key moments, sites, and actors in the cultures of the world before 1500. We discuss and critically engage with how historians craft their interpretations of the past using various sources: texts, objects, and ideas alike. Though a degree of mastery of basic facts is necessary, this course aims for the higher goal of enabling students to engage in the systematic analysis of changes, connections, and comparisons among premodern cultures. Offered every two ro three years.

subject: History
description: Development of state, society and culture of ancient Egypt, from beginnings through absorption of Egypt into Roman Empire. Original source material in translation.

subject: History
description: An introduction to the major civilizations of Mesopotamia (Sumerians, Babylonians, Assyrians), Syria-Palestine (Canaanites, Phoenicians, Israelites), Anatolia (Hittites, Urartians) and Iran (Medes and Persians) during the four millennia before the conquest by Alexander the Great. Emphasis on continuity and diversity, as well as such specific issues as: urbanization, political organization, law imperialism, society, religion, literature and art. Considerable use of ancient documents and artifacts.

subject: History
description: This course examines the formation of Greek civilization (especially its Classical and Hellenistic periods), the social and economic factors that underpinned it, and the cultural and intellectual narratives that shaped its ideological perspectives. It will also explore how certain Greeks have defined self-hood through their encounters with foreign peoples in ways that have shaped modern concepts of the ?West? and ?East.? Key areas of focus are: Greek political systems, law, family, class, gender, slavery, and encounters with non-Greek peoples.

subject: History
course_name: The Rise and Fall of Rome
description: This survey course will examine the formation of the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire. Key topics are the Romans? political and military organization; Roman Italian cultural life: the formation of Roman provincial societies and their cultural expressions, especially in the Middle East; migrations within and outside the empire; Jews and Christians in the empire; slavery and slave supply; and the empire?s relationships with a broader Afro-Eurasian world system.

subject: History
description: Political, cultural, economic survey of early medieval Europe. Decline of Roman Empire, rise and development of Christianity, origins of medieval Europe, Carolingian Empire, Vikings, beginnings of feudal society.

subject: History
description: Political, cultural, economic survey of later medieval Europe. Reform movements in Church, Crusades, evolution of universities, 12th-century Renaissance, growth of national states.

subject: History
description: Covers France from the Renaissance monarchy of the late 15th century to the French Revolution of the late 18th century, including the wars of religion, the reign of Louis XIV, and the Enlightenment. Ranges from peasant revolts to queen regents, from burning witches to decapitating nobles.

subject: History
description: Covers the major political, social and cultural developments that shaped Germany between 1871 and the present. Although designed as a general survey, it also addresses two more specific questions through readings and films: How have post-war Germans made sense of their own history? And how has the Nazi period been integrated and contextualized within modern German history and historiography?

subject: History
description: This course is a survey of Imperial Russia from 1682 to 1917. Students examine the legacy of Peter the Great, the evolution of autocracy, modernization, imperial power, the intelligentsia, the nationalities problem, the Great Reforms, revolutionary and women’s movements, the Revolution of 1905, and the last attempts to consolidate tsarist authority.

subject: History
description:
This course introduces students to the history of Europe during the seventeenth century by framing key developments and events within the context of the Thirty Years? War. Topics include war and its effects upon communities, the relationship between soldiers and citizens, the emergence of the
early-modern fiscal-military state, the growth of European colonial systems and their impact on European economies and societies. Readings include a survey, scholarly articles, and primary sources. Offered once every 6-8 semesters.

subject: History
description: From our twenty-first-century perspective, medieval medical treatments have a reputation for being misguided, painful, and bizarre. While this course will confront the stranger aspects of medieval medicine, we will attempt to understand them according to the historical logic of pre-modern practices. We will explore points of convergence between Eastern and Western medicine, see how saints and doctors competed for popular authority, investigate the origins of the professional study of medicine, and discuss the impact of epidemics like the Black Death. We begin with Hippocrates and end around 1600 with Renaissance anatomists. Offered regularly.

subject: History
description: This course helps students appreciate how medical knowledge and practices are implicated in and influenced by social, political and economic forces, as well as how the concepts of health and disease, the relationships among hospitals, professions and patients, the character of therapeutics and the role of science, technology and industry have changed over time. The course focuses on medicine in the West since the early modern period and in America since the 18th Century. It also includes materials on pre-modern and non-Western medicines.

subject: History
description: This course considers the relationships between animals and human societies since prehistoric times. We will begin with a discussion of hunting, the domestication of animals, and representations of animals in early human history. We will then go on to examine the roles of animals in food, culture, agriculture, and commerce in traditional societies. Specific examples may include food taboos in major religions, horses in Eurasia and the New World, and other comparative cases. The last part of the course will deal with the modern era. Topics may include the development of modern sensibilities toward animals; the impact of evolutionary theory on modern perceptions of animals (e.g. rethinking human/animal boundaries); representations of animals in popular culture; animals as pets; zoos, museums, sea worlds, and other institutions for displaying animals; wildlife preservation movements; and animal protection movements (including animal ethics).

subject: History
description: Examines world environmental history from prehistoric times to the present, with emphasis on the past 500 years. Begins by looking at the ancient agricultural civilizations and other modes of human societies in the world, then examines the environmental history of medieval Europe and of imperial China. The bulk of the course is devoted to studying European expansion and ecological imperialism, environmental history of late imperial and modern China, and American environmental history. Considers the rise of local and international conservation movements and environmentalism, ongoing environmental changes (for example, the Green Revolution, rapid population growth and urbanization in developing countries, etc.) and the important question of where we are heading.

subject: History
description: Aims to deepen understanding of science and technology by situating them in a world-historical context. Instead of focusing on individual discoveries or inventions, students examine the social meanings of science and technology in the modern world. They investigate issues such as the role of science and technology in European imperialism, the reception and development of science and technology in non-Western societies, the configurations of modernity in different societies and the anxieties toward science and technology reflected in art and literature. They also explore the complex reactions to certain developments in science and technology (e.g., Darwin’s theory of evolution, nuclear energy, artificial intelligence, genetic engineering). Finally, they consider the issue of globalization in relation to science and technology.

subject: History
description: Jewish history from fall of Second Temple to expulsion from Spain. Medieval Jewish communities within Islamic oikoumene; communities within Byzantine and Latin Christendom. Economic and social evolution, religious, intellectual, literary life during period that saw veritable crystallization and formulation of Judaism.

subject: History
description:
This course examines the practices and methods of history as an academic discipline. It investigates various approaches to the discipline and how it has developed over time with an emphasis on the last three hundred years. Students are exposed to research methods, historiographical and source
analysis, library skills, proper citation and writing methods, and major theoretical approaches to the study of history. The class also explores various career opportunities available to history majors. Students are assessed through various writing assignments, including a research paper proposal, annotated bibliography, scholarly literature review, and a research paper. Restriction: Preference given to History majors and minors. Offered each semester.

subject: History
description:
This introductory course surveys the history of Asians in the Americas with an emphasis on the mid?19th century to the present. The course explores the experiences of diverse Asian Americans from a global perspective and
examines primary and secondary sources. Offered at least once a year.

subject: History
description:
Sexual attitudes, desires, behaviors, communities, movements and identities have undergone profound transformations in American history. We will explore these developments and changes in
the history of sexuality over the last four hundred years, and examine the relationship between sexuality and class, ethnicity, gender identity, race, and religion; and the ways in which the study of sexuality offers opportunities to re-think major themes in U.S. social, cultural, and political history. The goal is to understand factors that shaped sexual lives, including customs and taboos, law, religion, medical expertise, and state policies. Offered Regularly.

subject: History
description: This course is a survey of American Women’s history from pre-settlement to present. While the course is not a history of feminism, students will use a feminist analysis to examine women’s roles and their impact on American history. Topics will include sexual exploitation; reproduction; “natural” gender roles; the sexual division of labor; class and race conflict; women’s work; sexual orientation; and women in the media. Readings will focus on the diversity of women’s  experiences and address the complexity of assuming a “shared” female experience in light of diverse race, class, and religious  differences, and sexual preference.

subject: History
description: Comparative histories of Asian Americans in the U.S. from 1850 to the 1990s. Themes include Asian migration, labor and ethnic enterprise, gender, family, community organization, anti-Asian movements, resistance, debates over citizenship.

subject: History
description: A narrative of U.S. history, emphasizing dynamic relationship of Native American cultures and history to European Americans, African Americans and Latinos in development of American pluralism. Focus on aboriginal cultures of North America and social and cultural changes that resulted from interactions with other ethnic/racial groups in U.S. Comparison and contrast of dynamics and results of Native American cultures’ interactions with European American, African American and Latino groups through time. Evaluation of impact of Native American cultures on global and national processes of change and how that impact altered over time. Role of Native Americans in American institutions, ideology and belief.

subject: History
description: This course examines post?reform China in a historical and global perspective. China has become a prominent presence in newspapers, TV broadcast, cultural references, and political discussions in this country and indeed internationally. All agree that when it comes to China, there is much to talk about, but few agree on what China is and what it will become. What happened during China’s economic reform in the late 1970s and early 1980s? Why and how did China’s economy grow so fast in the past couple of decades? With the growth of its economic power, China is playing an increasing role in international affairs. What does this mean to its neighboring states and beyond? Networks of Chinese migrants and traders have made their impact felt not only in Asia, but also in Europe, Africa, and Latin America. Internally, Chinese society and culture has gone through dramatic changes in one generation, and the phenomena of internal migration, urbanization, youth culture, growing economic inequality, new nationalism, environmental degradation, and economic challenges have exploded onto the scene. None of these phenomena can be understood in isolation from the contemporary world as China is part of an ever?intensified web of global interdependencies. (This course assumes no prior knowledge of Chinese history or language.) Offered Regularly.

subject: History
description: Political, social, economic and cultural survey of Chinese history from beginnings of Chinese civilization in second millennium BCE to the end of Ming dynasty. Topics include early formation of Chinese civilization, flowering of philosophy during the Zhou, impact of Buddhism, impact of alien dynasties, changes in landholding, southward expansion of Chinese culture and evolution of examination system. Readings draw primarily from Chinese historical, philosophical and literary texts in translation.

subject: History
description: A survey of the history of China’s last two imperial dynasties, the Ming and Qing (1368-1911). Topics include state-building in the aftermath of Mongol rule, the Zheng He maritime expeditions, factional strife and urban culture of the late Ming, the rise of the Manchus, the Jesuit mission to China, evidentiary learning, economy and society in the high Qing, population pressures, corruption and rebellion in the 19th Century; Western imperialism and attempts at reform; and revolutionary movements.

subject: History
description: The purpose of this course is to trace and investigate the history of the Modern Middle East from 1800-present through course lecture, discussion, and the reading of secondary and primary sources. Students are assessed through their preparation for and participation in discussion and through two midterm take home essays and a final paper. Topics to be considered include the integration of the Middle East into the modern world system; the nature, impact, and lasting effects of European imperialism; the legacies of the Ottoman and Qajar Empires for the modern Middle East; World War I and its effects; the origins and evolution of nationalism and the Middle East state system; Decolonization; the Revolutions of Mid-Century; the Arab-Israeli dispute; the effects of oil exploitation; the Iranian Revolution, Religion and Politics, the Arab uprisings and its aftermath, the Middle East Refugee Crisis, as well as the US relationship to the region.

subject: History
description: Overview of 19th- and 20th-century Latin America. Topics include independence movements and nation formation; export economies; political ideologies; slavery and emancipation; repression and resistance; revolutions and social movements; and inter-American relations. Dynamics of race, class and gender are considered throughout. Students develop skills in analyzing documentary sources, evaluating scholarly texts and writing essays.

subject: History
description: This interdisciplinary course provides an introduction to Latin America and the Caribbean, emphasizing the region’s history, politics, society, and culture. It considers the historical effects of colonial legacies and U.S. intervention. Topics may include: the state; colonialism and anti-colonialism; race and ethnicity; social movements; gender. The course will introduce various approaches to studying Latin America.  Offered every Fall.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 511: Biostatistics
This course introduces students to the concepts and methods of biostatistics. The skills learned in this course build the quantitative foundation that students will apply to evaluate the biomedical literature and assess its applicability to their patients. Descriptive statistics, inferential statistics, and hypothesis testing will be presented. Non-parametric methods, simple and multivariable regression methods, and survival analyses used in evaluating outcomes associated with pharmacologic therapies and other medical interventions in populations will be introduced. Emphasis will be placed on developing skills for the correct interpretation and evaluation of results. () 
Prerequisites: Pre-pharmacy curriculum and admission to the pharmacy program.
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 512: Pharmacy Law
This course provides an overview of the federal and state systems of government and emphasizes how laws are enacted and executed as well as how cases are adjudicated within these two systems. Additionally, the course provides a more detailed analysis of various federal and state laws that impact the practice of pharmacy in the United States along with a discussion of the public policy reasons and debates underlying those laws. As well, key regulations affecting drug development and distribution will be discussed. The laws and practices of New York will be used as primary examples of the types of laws and practices that generally exist within the individual states. ()
Prerequisites: Matriculation to the pharmacy program, PHRM 510
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 513: Pharmaceutics I: Physical Pharmacy
Basic concepts in physical pharmacy and pharmaceutical sciences including solubility, stability, permeability, properties and behaviors of gases and electrolyte and non-electrolyte solutions, and solid forms including dissolution and drug release are introduced in this first in a series of pharmaceutics courses. Achieving proficiency in these basic concepts of physical pharmacy will provide students with essential knowledge used and considerations taken in design and development of pharmaceutical dosage forms and drug delivery systems and in contemporary pharmacy practice. Specific types of dosage forms and the excipients used to produce them will also be discussed. () 
Prerequisites: Matriculation to the pharmacy program.
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 514: Pharmaceutical Calculations I
The ability to accurately perform pharmaceutical calculations is essential to providing safe patient care in virtually all pharmacy practice settings. Basic concepts and skills required to accurately perform pharmaceutical calculations required in pharmaceutical dosing and compounding are introduced in this first of two pharmaceutical calculations courses. Application of key mathematical principles to pharmaceutical calculations encountered in pharmacy practice is the primary focus of this course. Examples of such applications include the correct interpretation of prescription and medication administration orders, pharmaceutical measurements, mathematical manipulations involved in converting and preparing desired concentrations and strengths of electrolyte and isotonic solutions. Students will work/self-learn in small groups on representative calculation problems with adequate opportunity to receive assistance from faculty.
Prerequisites: Matriculation to the pharmacy program.
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 515: Pharmaceutics II: Dosage Forms and Drug Delivery
In this second in a series of pharmaceutics courses, the basic concepts developed in Pharmaceutics I (PHRM 513) are used as a foundation for students to further expand their learning about properties of dosage forms and drug delivery systems typically employed to administer medications. Specifically, technical and scientific considerations and methodologies required to produce dosage forms on a large scale, as well as the relationship of basic drug development and approval processes are covered. Emphasis is placed on understanding basic pharmaceutics principles underpinning representative dosage forms and delivery systems as well as their advantages and disadvantages. () 
Prerequisites: PHRM 513
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 516: Pharmaceutical Calculations II
The ability to accurately perform pharmaceutical calculations is essential to providing safe patient care in virtually all pharmacy practice settings. In this second of two pharmaceutical calculations courses, students will apply the basic concepts and skills learned in Pharmaceutical Calculations I (PHRM 514) to selected dosing and clinical calculations, intravenous infusion and parenteral admixture solutions preparation calculations, and calculations used in extemporaneous compounding. Students will work/self-learn in small groups on representative calculation problems with adequate opportunity to receive assistance from faculty. 
Prerequisites: PHRM 514
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM  520: Integrated Pharmacotherapy II: Gastrointestinal Disease
This is the second in a sequence of nine Integrated Pharmacotherapy modules with a focus on the gastrointestinal system and its diseases and disorders. Basic biochemical, anatomical and physiological, pharmacological, medicinal chemistry, pharmacokinetic, clinical chemistry and pharmacotherapeutic principles are integrated and applied to presentation and management of gastrointestinal conditions and diseases such as gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel syndrome , nausea and vomiting, dehydration, diarrhea, constipation, nutritional deficiencies, cirrhosis, drug induced gastrointestinal disease, pancreatitis, anemia, and viral hepatitis. Biological and physicochemical principles related to drug delivery and dosage forms used in the treatment of these disorders are covered as well as preparation methods and routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management of gastrointestinal diseases and disorders.
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 503 
This course is offered every Fall semester.

description:
PHRM 521: Integrated Pharmacotherapy III: Cardiology
This is the third in a sequence of nine Integrated Pharmacotherapy modules with a focus on the cardiovascular system and its diseases and disorders. Basic biochemical, anatomical and physiological, pharmacological, medicinal chemistry, pharmacokinetic, clinical chemistry and pharmacotherapeutic principles are integrated and applied to presentation and management of cardiovascular conditions and diseases such as hypertension, lipid disorders, chronic heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias. Biological and physicochemical principles related to drug delivery and dosage forms used in the treatment of these disorders are covered as well as preparation methods routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management of cardiovascular diseases and disorders. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 503
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 522: Integrated Pharmacotherapy IV: Endocrine, Renal and Reproductive Health
This is the fourth in a sequence of nine Integrated Pharmacotherapy modules with a focus on the endocrine, renal and reproductive systems and their diseases and disorders. Basic biochemical, anatomical and physiological, pharmacological, medicinal chemistry, pharmacokinetic, clinical chemistry and pharmacotherapeutic principles are integrated and applied to presentation and management of endocrine, renal and reproductive system conditions and diseases such as diabetes, thyroid and adrenal disorders, kidney disease, and benign prostatic hyperplasia as well as contraception and hormone replacement therapy. Biological and physicochemical principles related to drug delivery and dosage forms used in the treatment of these disorders are covered as well as preparation methods routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management of endocrine, renal and reproductive system diseases and disorders. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 503
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 523: Integrated Pharmacotherapy V: Neurology, Psychiatry and Anesthesiology
This is the fifth in a sequence of nine Integrated Pharmacotherapy modules with a focus on the nervous system and its diseases and disorders. Basic biochemical, anatomical and physiological, pharmacological, medicinal chemistry, pharmacokinetic, clinical chemistry and pharmacotherapeutic principles are integrated and applied to presentation and management of neurological and psychiatric conditions and diseases such as Alzheimer?s disease, Parkinson?s disease, epilepsy, pain management, headaches, sleep disorders, depression, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and substance use/misuse. Biological and physicochemical principles related to drug delivery and dosage forms used in the treatment of these disorders are covered as well as preparation methods routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management of neurological and psychiatric conditions and diseases. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 503
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 524: Integrated Pharmacotherapy VI: Infectious Disease
This is the sixth in a sequence of nine Integrated Pharmacotherapy modules with a focus on infectious diseases. Basic biochemical, microbiological, anatomical and physiological, pharmacological, medicinal chemistry, pharmacokinetic, clinical chemistry and pharmacotherapeutic principles are integrated and applied to presentation and management of infectious and fungal diseases such as respiratory tract infections, skin and soft tissue infections, bone and joint infections, urinary tract infections, central nervous system infections, endocarditis, sexually transmitted diseases, HIV/AIDS tuberculosis, and fungal infections. As well emphasis is placed on pathogen identification and antibiotic selection to achieve pathogen coverage. Biological and physicochemical principles related to drug delivery and dosage forms used in the treatment of infectious disease are covered as well as preparation methods and routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management of infectious diseases. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 503
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 525: SKILLS LAB - Integrated Pharmacotherapy II - IV: Concepts and Patient Care Skills
This course is a companion course to the Integrated Pharmacotherapy Courses II - IV (PHRM 520, 521, and 522) with a focus on students applying the foundational and clinical knowledge from these courses in hands-on activities and active-learning exercises in order to develop skills required for practice in clinical settings. Specifically, students will actively practice and participate in exercises designed to develop skills and competence in patient assessment (including triage and referral), formulation of viable patient-specific treatment recommendations and patient counseling techniques regarding pharmacotherapy and prevention. Further students will become familiar with NY prescription laws and regulations and drug schedules. Specifically, patient case presentations and simulations based on real-life clinical cases involving gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, endocrine, renal/urologic and reproductive conditions will be used to develop students? critical thinking skills with respect to patient presentation, documentation of patient history, patient assessment, formulation of treatment recommendation and medication monitoring for efficacy and toxicity. 
Prerequisites: PHRM 505
This course is offered every Fall semester.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 528: Population Health and Study Design Evaluation
This course is designed to introduce students to basic concepts of epidemiology and study designs used in the evaluation of health care technologies. Epidemiological terminology such as risk, hazard, odds and relative risk ratios will be introduced. An understanding of the use of epidemiologic methods in public health will be developed along with an exploration of the use of these methods in effecting health policy. Additionally, students will develop skills in the critical evaluation of evidence-based medical (EBM) literature and identification of sources of bias in published medical literature. EBM literature and population health combined with critical evaluation will be applied to inform clinical decisions at an individual patient level. () 
Prerequisites: PHRM 511
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 529: Drug Information and Health Informatics
This course focuses on the use of essential drug and toxicology information sources within contemporary pharmacy practice, building on evidence-based medicine (EBM) literature evaluation skills developed in earlier courses. Additionally, the course introduces students to the role of health information technology in health care delivery. Topics include primary, secondary and tertiary sources of drug information, medication safety, acute poisoning with emphasis on formulating drug information responses as well as an introduction to the use of drug monographs and key pharmaceutical information such as electronic medical records, e-prescribing and computerized physician order entry. () 
Prerequisites: PHRM 511, PHRM 528
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 530: Health Care Ethics (IPE Course )
This interactive course helps prepare pharmacy students to provide effective health care by applying ethical tenets in their relationships with patients and members of the health care team, discussing contemporary ethical issues encountered in the provision of patient-centered health care, using team problem-solving activities focused on ethical dilemmas encountered in medical decision-making, and examining the impact of culture and beliefs of the patient in medical decision-making. This is an interprofessional course and includes the interactions of students in different professions on the healthcare team. Students will participate in a significant project or clinical interprofessional experience involving conflicting ethical choices and prepare and present a team-based decision based on their experiences and interactions.
Prerequisites: Successful completion of the P1 year.
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 533: SKILLS LAB ? Pharmaceutical Compounding and Dispensing 
The ability to accurately prepare pharmaceutical drug dosage forms is essential to provide safe and efficacious therapy to patients. In pharmaceutical compounding and dispensing, the basic concepts and skills required to extemporaneously compound non-sterile products are introduced. Mathematical competencies will be assessed as will the students’ ability to compound accurate and pharmaceutically elegant dosage forms, and label these products correctly.  
Prerequisites: PHRM 515, PHRM 516 
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 534: Pharmaceutics III: Sterile Products and Biopharmaceuticals
Building upon basic concepts and skills developed in previous pharmaceutics and calculations courses, students will apply their knowledge and expand their skills to various sterile products including parenteral, ophthalmic, and TPN solutions. The course features both class and laboratory components, providing students hands-on experience in sterile product compounding. Biologic pharmaceuticals (monoclonal antibodies, vaccines and adjuvants) as well as various routes of administration, sterile product preparation and quality standards are covered in this course.
Prerequisites: PHRM 533
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy

routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist
students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management
of pulmonary system, eye, ear, nose and throat conditions and diseases. ()

Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 503, PHRM 524
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 542: Integrated Pharmacotherapy VIII: Hematology, Oncology, and Autoimmune Diseases 
This is the eighth in a sequence of nine Integrated Pharmacotherapy modules with a focus on hematological disorders, prevalent oncologic and autoimmune diseases. Basic biochemical, microbiological, anatomical and physiological, pharmacological, medicinal chemistry, pharmacokinetic, clinical chemistry and pharmacotherapeutic principles are integrated and applied to presentation and management of: (1) hematologic disorders such as anemias, select coagulation disorders and sickle cell disease; (2) oncologic disorders such as breast, prostate, lung, and colorectal cancers, acute and chronic leukemia, and lymphoma; (3) supportive therapy for oncologic care for tumor lysis syndrome, blood dyscrasias, gastrointestinal toxicities, bone health and oncologic emergencies; (4) major autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematous and rheumatoid arthritis as well as treatment in solid organ transplant. Biological and physicochemical principles related to drug delivery and dosage forms used in the treatment of hematological disorders, prevalent oncologic and autoimmune diseases are covered as well as preparation, methods and routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management of hematologic, oncologic, and autoimmune-related disease states. 
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 503
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 543: Integrated Pharmacotherapy IX: Special Populations ? Geriatrics, Pediatrics and Health of Rural Populations
This is the ninth in a sequence of nine Integrated Pharmacotherapy modules with a focus on diseases and disorders affecting geriatric, pediatric and rural populations. Basic biochemical, anatomical and physiological, pharmacological, medicinal chemistry, pharmacokinetic, clinical chemistry and pharmacotherapeutic principles are integrated and applied to presentation and management of disease and disorders common to these populations such as osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, delirium, critical care, end of life/palliative care, malnutrition, and dehydration. Additionally, differences in the presentation and treatment of different diseases (covered in previous Integrated Pharmacotherapy Courses) as well as adverse reactions to medications in these populations will be addressed. Biological and physicochemical principles related to drug delivery and dosage forms used in the treatment of these disorders are covered as well as preparation methods routes of administration. Examples and active case-based learning are used to assist students? building skills to solve problems associated with the treatment and management of conditions and diseases in these populations. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 504, PHRM 520, PHRM 521, PHRM 522, PHRM 523, PHRM 524, PHRM 541, PHRM 542
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 545: SKILLS/ SMALL GROUP COMPLEX CASES: Integrated Pharmacotherapy I ? IX: Whole System Overview Integrating Concepts and Advanced Patient Care
In preparation for progression into Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experiences (APPEs), the focus of this course is to help students integrate and apply prior learning from previous courses to formulate clinical solutions and care plan recommendations for treatment and management of diseases and disorders in patients with multiple comorbidities. Students will have hands-on opportunities to identify, assess and resolve disease-related problems in patients with multiple comorbidities through using a series of comprehensive cases based on real-world clinical cases; students will be guided and expected to apply their knowledge and critical thinking skills to recommend real-life clinical solutions. Comprehensive patient documentation will be used in students? preparation for patient case presentations and as a means of documenting key discussion points. Students will reinforce key clinical concepts and acquire skills in developing management and treatment plans for complex patient cases as final preparation for their progression into APPEs where they will encounter correspondingly complex patients. Additionally, students will participate in an IPE activity/simulation. ()

This course is offered every Spring semester.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 548: Pharmacoepidemiology, Pharmacoeconomics and Health Outcomes
This course is designed to familiarize students with the principles of pharmacoepidemiology and pharmacoeconomics. Focus is on major areas of the evolving fields of pharmacoepidemiology and pharmacoeconomics with an emphasis on measuring health outcomes. Course material builds on and extends the skills and concepts learned in previous courses within the curriculum (PHRM 528, PHRM 529) that are focused on the effectiveness of medication use at a population level. The additional dimensions of efficiency or cost relative to the benefit of a given health outcome and patient quality of life are introduced and developed. Use of pharmacoepidemiologic studies in post-marketing safety studies and communication of risk is covered. Additionally, the role of both pharmacoepidemiologic and pharmacoeconomic studies in the formulary process used for medication coverage by insurers and hospitals is explored. () 
Prerequisites: PHRM 511, PHRM 528, PHRM 529
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 550: Contemporary Pharmacy Leadership and Management
Organizational structures and cultures have an impact on the contemporary practice of pharmacy; a variety of stakeholders take an interest and have a voice in the professional practice of pharmacy. Pharmacists will need an awareness of managerial issues they will likely encounter in order to be effective practitioners. This course addresses these needs by introducing basic administrative, business, managerial and leadership principles necessary for the effective and efficient delivery of patient-centered care goals. As such the course complements the clinical and professional expertise pharmacy students have developed through completing integrated pharmacotherapy, population health and previous professional pharmacy practice courses. Course topics include budgetary and financial considerations, marketing principles, personnel management, customer service, continuous quality assessment and performance improvement as well as risk management and compliance with state and federal laws and regulations and quality standards proposed by accrediting agencies on pharmacy management and leadership. The impact of these areas to improved value propositions and improved patient safety is explored. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 510
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 551: Public Health and Global Health Problems
This course familiarizes students with public health concepts and practice at community, national and global levels with emphasis on global health problems as well as the expanding roles for pharmacists in public health. In particular, the roles for pharmacists in disaster preparedness and ensuring medication safety will be discussed. The course will include key historical learnings from public health, an exploration of the social determinants of health and the principles used in evidence-based public health practice. Understanding the evaluation of public health interventions will be a central course theme in combination with student investigation of major global public health issues in infectious and chronic disease. As well, students will explore key public health issues in the local and adjacent rural communities surrounding Binghamton, NY. Student exploration of public health problems will include student participation in case-based active learning exercises. (2 credits)
Prerequisites: PHRM 548
This course is offered every Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 553: Pharmacy, Pharmacogenomics and Precision Medicine
The focus of this course is on how genetic factors can modify pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic parameters of how a medication acts in different individuals and ultimately impact its efficacy and toxicity in different patients. Topics include pharmacogenomics principles and applications, biochemical analytical methods, clinical interpretation of laboratory data, and applied pharmacokinetics and therapeutic drug monitoring. Pharmacologic, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacotherapeutic underpinnings are highlighted. Emphasis is placed on considering genomic and phenotypic information to individualize pharmacotherapy and minimize adverse events. Economic and ethical issues relevant to incorporating pharmacogenomic data in the clinical decision-making process are discussed, particularly in the context of providing patient-centered care. 
Prerequisites: PHRM 502, PHRM 503, PHRM 528
This course is offered every Fall semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 554: Advanced Skills Lab ? Pharmaceutical Compounding

The course emphasizes compounding fundamentals across multiple dosage forms. Further, students will review NY Prescription laws and regulations and drug schedules. The focus is on helping students prepare for pharmacy practice.
Prerequisites: PHRM 533, PHRM 534
This course is offered every Spring semester.

This is the fourth introductory pharmacy practice experience (IPPE) and builds on students? exposure to pharmacy practice in a variety of direct patient care environments. The student is required to complete at least 300 hours of IPPE during the first three years; a minimum of 150 hours will be balanced between community pharmacy and institutional health-system settings. description:
PHRM 572: Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience I - Community Pharmacy:
This Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience (APPE) builds on the knowledge and skills students have acquired during their P1 ? P3 years through direct patient care experiences in a community practice setting. Key goals of all APPEs are to continue the development of students? critical thinking and problem-solving skills through ?hands-on? experiences. During this experience, students will actively take part in many community pharmacy practice activities/experiences including: interactions with patients, caregivers, prescribers, and insurers; patient counseling; self-care assessment and triage; alternative and herbal medicine consultation and recommendation; prescription filling, dispensing and verification processes; and health and wellness screenings and immunizations as appropriate. Goals of this APPE are to provide students with opportunities to: (1) develop knowledge and clinical skills in the provision of patient-centered care at the individual and patient population levels in a community practice setting; (2) build clinical decision-making skills and confidence in these skills; and (3) develop competent pharmacy management skills. (6 credits)
Prerequisites: Successful completion of P3 year and all Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experiences.
This course is offered in Fall, Winter, Spring and Summer.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 573: Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience II: Ambulatory Care Pharmacy
This Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience (APPE) builds on the knowledge and skills students have acquired during their P1 ? P3 years through direct patient care in an ambulatory care practice setting, with a focus on provision of care for patients with Ambulatory Care-Sensitive Conditions (ACSCs). Key goals of all APPEs are to continue the development of students? critical thinking and problem-solving skills through ?hands-on? experiences. During this experience, students will actively take part in many ambulatory care pharmacy practice activities/experiences including: individualized patient counseling; ongoing drug therapy monitoring; medication therapy management as appropriate; patient education material development; and active collaboration with other healthcare professionals in the drug therapy decision-making process. The goals of this APPE are to provide students with opportunities to: (1) develop knowledge and clinical skills in the provision of patient-centered care at the individual and ACSCs patient population level; (2) build clinical decision-making skills and confidence in these skills; (3) develop safe, cost-effective and individualized patient care plans which may be documented in the patient?s medical record and implemented through communication with the patient and providers; and (4) monitor care plans through collection and interpretation of patient data including patient interviews. (6 credits)
Prerequisites: Successful completion of P3 year and all Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experiences.
This course is offered in Fall, Winter, Spring and Summer.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Pharmacy

PHRM 574: Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience III: Pharmacy Administration/Institutional
This Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience (APPE) builds on the knowledge and skills students have acquired during their P1 ? P3 years through direct patient care in an inpatient pharmacy administration/institutional setting, with a focus on central pharmacy and medication distribution functions. Key goals of all APPEs are to continue the development of students? critical thinking and problem-solving skills through ?hands-on? experiences. During this experience, students will actively take part in pharmacy practice activities/experiences within hospital/health system pharmacy including: the medication use process; quality assurance; medication safety; interprofessional collaboration; preparation of sterile and nonsterile medication, and parenteral nutrition products. The goals of this APPE are to provide students with opportunities to: (1) develop knowledge and clinical skills in the provision of patient-centered care within a hospital/institutional pharmacy practice setting; (2) build clinical decision-making skills and confidence in these skills; (3) provide safe, accountable patient care through thorough knowledge of informatics, medication distribution and documentation processes; and (4) develop pharmacy management skills. (6 credits)
Prerequisites: Successful completion of P3 year and all Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experiences.
This course is offered in Fall, Winter, Spring and Summer.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 575: Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience IV: General/Internal Medicine
This Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experience (APPE) builds on the knowledge and skills students have acquired during their P1 ? P3 years through direct patient care experiences in an inpatient general medicine/internal medicine acute care setting. Key goals of all APPEs are to continue development of students? critical thinking and problem-solving skills through ?hands-on? experiences. During this experience, students will actively take part in many pharmacy practice activities/experiences occurring within a general medicine/internal medicine acute care setting. Examples of these activities/experiences include: optimizing drug therapy management and medication safety in acute care; drug therapy monitoring to establish efficacy and prevent adverse events in high acuity and potentially quickly-changing medical situations; and participating as a member of the interprofessional healthcare team. Goals of this APPE are to provide students with opportunities to: (1) develop knowledge and clinical skills in the provision of patient-centered care within an acute care pharmacy practice setting with rapidly changing clinical requirements; (2) build clinical decision-making skills and confidence in these skills; and (3) provide safe, individualized and accountable patient care from hospital admission through discharge as part of an interprofessional healthcare team in an acute medical care setting. (6 credits)
Prerequisites: Successful completion of P3 year and all Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experiences.
This course is offered in Fall, Winter, Spring and Summer.   Course Fees  Course fee applies. Refer to the Schedule of Classes.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580A: Medical Marijuana
This course is an elective covering medical marijuana with a focus on history, pharmacology, pharmacotherapeutics, and legal considerations. Basic botanical, biochemical, physiological, pharmacological, pharmacokinetic, pharmacotherapeutic, public health, testing limitations, ethical considerations, and legal principles are applied to the production, utilization, monitoring, and complications of adverse advents of medical marijuana. Biological and physicochemical processes related to drug delivery and dosage forms of medical marijuana are covered as well as preparation methods and routes of administration. Active case-based learning, in-class debate, self-reflection, and longitudinal projects are used to assist students in building skills to solve problems associated with the use of medical marijuana for the treatment and management of a myriad of disease states. Additionally, the course will address legal and public health considerations as they apply to patients and the general public. ()
Prerequisites: Completion of the Pharmacy Year 1 curriculum and matriculation to Pharmacy Year 2
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580B: Complementary and Alternative Medicine
This elective course explores the role of selected complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) therapies used world-wide for the attainment of health. The World Health Organization definition of health will be emphasized. CAM and allopathic medicine will be compared and their combined use will be discussed with the introduction of the Integrative Medicine approach to patient-centered care. The scientific evidence regarding effectiveness and safety will be discussed with each of the CAM therapies presented. With the discussion of cultural health belief practices, students will be introduced to the idea that our personal health beliefs interplay with our cultural and traditional life experiences to inform our preventative and curative health behaviors. ()
Prerequisites: Completion of the Pharmacy Year 1 curriculum and matriculation to Pharmacy Year 2.
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580C: Cellular and Molecular Basis of Disease
This elective course will provide and reinforce foundational knowledge in the pathophysiology and molecular basis of human disease using representative disease examples to illustrate key principles. Students will learn to link fundamental genetic, molecular and cellular components of disease to primary and secondary aspects of disease pathogenesis in select organ systems. Students will learn to read, evaluate and discuss selected primary research and review articles addressing the cellular and molecular basis of disease. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580D: Healthy Lifestyle Interventions
Healthy Lifestyle Interventions is an elective course that explores components of a healthy lifestyle from biological and human behavioral perspectives. The goal is to define and understand unhealthy behaviors and their persistence, and to learn and apply the neurobiology of behavioral modification to promote healthy lifestyles. Topics of study include concepts such as nutrition, kinesiology, sleep, stress, reward/addiction, relationships/peer support, and attitude/self-efficacy. Students will apply these concepts in a longitudinal project where they practice these approaches in their own life. () 
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502
This course can be offered in either Spring or Fall.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580E: Drug Discovery
This elective course will provide an in-depth overview of the drug-discovery process, particularly from the perspective of the modern pharmaceutical and biotech industry. Students will gain insight into the: (1) the selection of drug targets; (2) identification of lead molecules; (3) role of animal models of human diseases; (4) optimization of potency and pharmacokinetics; (5) assessment of drug safety and drug-drug interactions; (6) financial risks and rewards associated with drug development; (7) drug approval process; and (8) regulatory and intellectual property issues. A major emphasis of the class will be on case studies that illustrate these principles. Case studies will emphasize drugs that the students are familiar with from their IPT classes. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502, PHRM 510
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580F: Jump Start into Residency:
This elective course is designed to reinforce and build upon skills necessary for student pharmacists to excel as professionals throughout the remainder of the pharmacy curriculum, including Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experiences (APPEs), and their professional career. Throughout this course, students will identify their strengths and personality characteristics that are related to and affect their development of professional skills and competencies, evaluate and effectively communicate medical literature, apply newly published literature and guideline recommendations to improve patient care, and increase confidence about post-graduate residency training. Emphasis will be placed upon short lectures, group discussions, and active-learning strategies, such as small-group exercises, journal clubs, drug monograph reviews, presentations and mock P&T committee meetings. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 528, PHRM 529. 
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring semester.

subject: Pharmacy
course_name: Crit Thinking and Comm in R&D
description:
PHRM 580G: Critical Thinking and Communication in Research and Drug Development:
This elective course will focus on the development of written and oral skills for communicating and evaluating scientific research and drug development ideas and findings to different audiences. Students will learn to link fundamental concepts in critical thinking to evaluate their own ideas/findings and those of others.  Students will advance their skills in reading, evaluating and discussing selected articles and sources. ()
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, 502, 528. 
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580H: Toxicology & Drug Induced Disease: 
This course is an elective covering toxicology and drug induced diseases with a focus on pharmacovigilance, altered pharmacokinetics, xenobiotic toxicities, and the monitoring/treatment of drug induced diseases. Basic physiological, pharmacological, pharmacokinetic, pharmacotherapeutic, public health, and legal principles are applied to the monitoring, detection, treatment, and complications of xenobiotic toxicities and drug induced diseases. Case-based learning, classroom group work, patient simulation, and longitudinal projects are used to assist students in building skills to solve problems associated with the prevention, detection, monitoring, and treatment of xenobiotic toxicities and drug induced diseases. Additionally, the course will address public health considerations pertinent to the prevention and detection of xenobiotic toxicities and drug induced diseases.
()
Prerequisite: PHRM 529
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580I: Advanced Infectious Diseases Pharmacotherapy: 
This elective course is designed to build upon and supplement the core infectious disease content learned in PHRM 524 (Infectious Diseases Integrated Pharmacotherapeutics). Students will actively engage in various learning activities to provide advanced pharmacotherapeutic management of patients with various infectious diseases. Antimicrobial stewardship principles will be emphasized and applied in a variety of formats and scenarios. Infectious disease related public health issues will be reviewed as well as their impact on the management of specific patient populations. The epidemiology, clinical microbiology, pathophysiology, and antimicrobial management of selected infectious diseases will be further explored. 
() 
Prerequisite: PHRM 524.
This course can be offered in either Fall or Spring.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580J: The Rural and Underserved Service Track (TRUST): This course builds upon the contents that are delivered in The Rural and Underserved Service Track (TRUST) through learning retreats and service activities. TRUST students are given the opportunity to discuss perceptions, challenges, and techniques associated with specific underserved populations, including and expanding beyond the eight populations discussed in the TRUST learning retreat curriculum. Populations explored include the homeless, immigrants/refugees, incarcerated, children, older adults, veterans, individuals with substance use or mental health disorders, individuals with intellectual and developmental disorders, individuals who identify as LGBTQ+, as well as others  identified by students enrolled as appropriate. Students develop and propose future implementation of a unique, interprofessional service project that will be incorporated into the TRUST curriculum. All course components emphasize helping students understand the roles and contributions of pharmacists in primary care and with underserved patients, developing skills in drug therapy management and direct patient care as they apply to real-world practicalities when caring for underserved patients. Additionally, students will continue developing communication, teamwork, and leadership skills that enable effective collaboration with members of other health care professions. (). Requires department permission.
Prerequisites: PHRM 501, PHRM 502
This course can be offered in either Spring or Fall.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580K: Advanced Pediatric Pharmacotherapy: This elective course is designed to build upon and supplement the core pediatrics disease content learned in PHRM 541 IPT VII: Pulmonary, Eye, Ear, Nose and Throat and PHRM 543 IPT IX: Special Populations ? Geriatrics, Pediatrics, and Health of Rural Populations. Pharmacotherapeutic principles are applied to the presentation and management of pediatric patients with various disorders. Students will also engage in learning activities related to the pharmacist?s role in the pediatric advanced life support resuscitation team, medication safety, family medication education, and advocacy for pediatric patients. ()
Corequisite: PHRM 543 
This course can be offered in Spring or Fall.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580L: Special Topics in Family Medicine.
This elective course is designed to build upon and supplement knowledge of common, long-term illnesses encountered in ambulatory and hospital family medicine practice. Students will actively engage in various learning activities to apply the Pharmacists’ Patient Care Process to advanced pharmacotherapeutic inpatient and outpatient management of disorders which may include (but not limited to) diabetes, anticoagulation, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, heart failure, polypharmacy, COPD or asthma, pain, acute kidney injury, and chronic kidney disease. The focus will be on holistic care, transitions of care, and continuity across the family life cycle. In addition, students will explore ambulatory and institutional pharmacist patient care models and pharmacist provider status. Students will develop tools and practice skills to improve success on their APPEs. (). 
Prerequisites: Completion of the Pharmacy Year 2 curriculum and matriculation to Pharmacy Year 3, PHRM 528, PHRM 529.
This course can be offered in either Spring or Fall.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580M: Advanced Psychiatric Pharmacotherapy:
This elective course is designed to build upon and supplement the core psychiatric content learned in PHRM 523 (Neurology, Psychiatry, and Anesthesiology Integrated Pharmacotherapeutics). Students will actively engage in learning activities to provide  advanced pharmacotherapeutic management of mental health and neuropsychiatry disorders as they relate to the practice of pharmacy in the clinical setting.  The specialized role of the pharmacist in the treatment of patients with psychiatric conditions will be discussed, including the opportunities for fostering interprofessional relationships with other health care providers.  Students will gain a historical and cultural perspective on the treatment of psychiatric patients, evaluate and present on key clinical drug trials, review current treatment guidelines, and develop pharmacotherapeutic plans for the management of psychiatric conditions beyond what is covered in PHRM 523. ()
Pre-requisites: PHRM 523, PHRM 526
This course can be offered in Spring of Fall

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580N: World Citizenship and Global Health:
This course introduces the concept of the global citizen, the interconnectedness of all peoples, and social responsibility. Students will gain abetter understanding of global health care disparities and challenges as well as learn about the leading causes of illness, disability and death. The ethics of short-term medical trips as well as remaining healthy and safe during international travel will be discussed. This course supports the development of culturally aware healthcare professionals. Objectives will be met through engaging classroom activities as well as key projects. ()
Prerequisite: Completion of the Pharmacy Year 1 curriculum and matriculation to Pharmacy Year 2
This course can be offered in either Spring or Fall

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580 P: Advanced Cardiovascular Pharmacotherapy: This elective course is designed to cover advanced cardiovascular disease pharmacotherapy topics which may include but are not limited to, acute coronary syndromes, arrhythmias, cardiac surgery, valvular heart disease, advanced hemodynamics, electrophysiology, and pulmonary hypertension. The course is a blend of didactic teaching, journal clubs, simulations, and case-based discussions and will further explore and expand upon concepts learned in Cardiology Integrated Pharmacotherapy. Course topics will include both acute and chronic management, however, inpatient cardiovascular disease management will be emphasized. Approximately 1 hour each week will be dedicated to flipped classroom lecture, 1 hour to journal club presentations, and 1 hour on case based discussion; however, there will be some variability in course structure depending on the topic covered.  ()
This course can be offered in either Spring or Fall
Prerequisite: PHRM 521

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580Q: Nutrition, Microbiome and Drug Interactions in Health and Disease
This elective course will explore the intricate connections between nutrition, the microbiome and drug therapy in health and disease. It will include general principles of nutrition, microbiome changes over the life cycle, and emerging research findings in the interactions of nutrition and drug therapy on microbiome in health and various diseases. Students will gain insight into: 1) the pivotal and dynamic role of nutrition and the microbiome in overall health; 2) the impact of perturbations in nutrition/medications and the microbiome in disease development or representative disease states; and 3) the potential applications of nutritional and/or microbiome therapies in disease prevention and management. Students will engage in various course learning activities, including research and review article discussions, individual projects to deepen understanding of course concepts, and group projects that integrate knowledge into practical applications. 
Prerequisite: Completion of the Pharmacy Year 1 curriculum and matriculation to Pharmacy Year 2
This course can be offered in either Spring or Fall.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580R: Managed Care Pharmacy:
This elective course is designed to help future pharmacists learn more about and prepare for a career in the field of managed care. However, since the principles of managed care are applicable throughout pharmacy practice, this course will help future pharmacists interested in any area of practice better understand the clinical and business decision-making processes of the health care system. The elective will introduce and reinforce the concepts of population health and value, explore tools available to limit healthcare spending, and discuss unique ways pharmacists can be involved in improving patient care. 
Prerequisite: Completion of the Pharmacy Year 1 curriculum and matriculation to Pharmacy Year 2
This course can be offered in either Spring or Fall.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 580S: Regulatory Science in Drug Development This course will provide an in-depth overview of regulatory science as practice during drug
development. The primary focus will be on the US regulatory system (FDA), with additional training in the European system (EMA). The nature and mechanics of the interactions between the drug developer (Sponsor) and regulatory body (FDA) will be explained, and then practiced through a series
of role-playing tutorials using the vamorolone drug approval pathway as an exemplar. The original documents from the vamorolone program, from pre-IND, Phase I to Phase II transition, Phase II to Phase III transition, and pre-NDA meetings will be studied. Current controversies in regulatory
science will be studied in parallel, as a means of emphasizing critical aspects of the regulatory rationale utilized through the clinical drug development pipeline. [] 
Prerequisite: Completion of the Pharmacy Year 1 curriculum and matriculation to Pharmacy Year 2
This course can be offered in Fall or Spring.

subject: Pharmacy
description:
PHRM 587: Professional Development and Practice Readiness I
This is the first of a two-part course series. The focus of these courses is to foster the skills, attitudes and values necessary for pharmacist self-directed learning and focused preparation for licensure.  Students will participate in activities and events to initiate the development of professional relationships and begin to establish a professional network. Students will meet individually with faculty to review a personal mission statement and discuss potential career opportunities after graduation. In this first course (PHRM 587), students update their CV/resume, practice interviewing, continue updating their ePortfolios, start a program of practice licensure assessments, and build a plan to complete the steps for licensure as well as demonstrate their professional and career preparedness. (2  credits)
Prerequisites: Successful completion of P3 year and all Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experiences.
This course is offered every Fall semester.

This is the second of a two-part course series. The focus of these courses is to foster the skills, attitudes and values necessary for pharmacist self-directed learning and focused preparation for licensure.  Students will participate in activities and events to initiate the development of professional relationships and begin to establish a professional network. Students will meet individually with faculty to review a personal mission statement and discuss potential career opportunities after graduation. In this second course (PHRM 588), students continue updating their ePortfolios, complete practice licensure assessments, and participate in formal Board reviews as well as demonstrate their professional and career preparedness. 
(2 credits ).
